JavaScript was created at Netscape in 1995 by Brendan Eich in ten days, originally under the name Mocha and then LiveScript, and renamed JavaScript for marketing reasons even though it has almost nothing to do with Java. Microsoft responded with JScript, and the resulting incompatibilities pushed the language into a standards body. In 1997 the first edition of ECMA-262 appeared, defining a language called ECMAScript. JavaScript is the practical implementation of that standard, and the names are used almost interchangeably today.

The standard is versioned by year since 2015: ES2015 or ES6 introduced classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, let, const and generators in one large release, and every year since adds smaller features. Engines implement features incrementally, and compatibility tables show which features are available where. When documentation says something is a proposal, it may be usable behind a flag or in the newest engines, but it is not yet guaranteed for production.

### Code

The seven primitive types and the one structural type, checked at run time:

```js
console.log(
  typeof 1,          // 'number'
  typeof 1n,         // 'bigint'
  typeof 'a',        // 'string'
  typeof true,       // 'boolean'
  typeof undefined,  // 'undefined'
  typeof Symbol(),   // 'symbol'
  typeof null,       // 'object'  <- the famous historical bug
  typeof {},         // 'object'
  typeof (() => {}), // 'function'
);
```

The single number type is a 64-bit float, which is why the classic decimal case fails:

```js
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);              // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);      // false
console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON);  // true
```

And the three special numbers that are not errors:

```js
console.log(1 / 0, -1 / 0, 0 / 0);   // Infinity -Infinity NaN
console.log(NaN === NaN);            // false — NaN is not equal to itself
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN));    // true
```

### Where JavaScript runs

JavaScript needs a host environment that provides an engine plus platform APIs. In a browser the engine is embedded in the browser and the host APIs are the DOM, fetch, storage, canvas, and events. Outside the browser, Node.js embeds the V8 engine and provides file system, network, and process APIs; Deno and Bun offer similar capabilities with different defaults and tooling. The core language is the same everywhere, but the available globals differ, which is the single most common source of confusion when moving code between environments.

Because the language core is shared, code can be written once and adapted with feature detection. The rule of thumb is that syntax and built-in objects come from ECMAScript and are portable, while anything reached through window, document, process, or Deno is host-specific. A well-structured project isolates the host-specific parts so the reasoning code stays portable.

### Design character and goals

JavaScript is dynamically typed, prototype-based, single-threaded with an event loop, and multi-paradigm. It borrows syntax from Java and C, first-class functions from Scheme, and prototypes from Self. Values carry their type at runtime rather than being declared, objects inherit from other objects rather than from classes in the classical sense, and functions are ordinary values that can be stored, passed and returned.

The language favours permissiveness and backwards compatibility. It coerces types in surprising ways, never removes old features, and prefers to keep old pages working rather than to break them. This means a modern style is partly a matter of discipline: use strict mode, prefer const, compare with the strict equality operator, and treat coercing operators with care. Mastering JavaScript is largely learning which of its permissive behaviours are useful and which are traps.

JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Primitives are immutable and are compared by value, so two equal strings are equal. Everything else, including objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps and regular expressions, is a reference value of type object. The typeof operator reports the kind of a value, with two historical exceptions: typeof null returns the string object, and typeof of a function returns function even though functions are objects.

Because primitives are copied but objects are shared by reference, passing an object to a function lets that function mutate the caller's data, while passing a number cannot. Understanding this distinction is the root of most aliasing bugs. Copying an object requires an explicit shallow copy with spread or Object.assign, or a deep copy with structuredClone for values that contain only cloneable data.

### Code

The `+` operator concatenates if either side is a string, and `-` always converts to a number. That asymmetry is the source of most bugs:

```js
console.log(1 + 2 + '3');     // '33'   left to right
console.log('3' + 1 + 2);     // '312'
console.log('6' - 1);         // 5
console.log('6' * '2');       // 12
console.log([] + {});         // '[object Object]'
console.log({} + []);         // '[object Object]'  (both sides become strings)
console.log([] + 1);          // '1'
console.log(+[]);             // 0
```

Falsy values are exactly these seven, and everything else — including `'0'`, `[]` and `{}` — is truthy:

```js
const falsy = [false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN];
console.log(falsy.map(Boolean));            // all false
console.log(Boolean('0'), Boolean(' '), Boolean([]), Boolean({}));  // true true true true
```

`ToPrimitive` is the operation underneath, and you can take control of it:

```js
class Money {
  constructor(cents) { this.cents = cents; }
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
    if (hint === 'string') return `$${(this.cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
    return this.cents;
  }
}

const price = new Money(1999);
console.log(`${price}`);      // $19.99
console.log(price + 1);       // 2000
```

### Implicit coercion

Coercion converts a value from one type to another. Explicit coercion is deliberate, as in Number(text) or String(value). Implicit coercion happens when an operator expects a particular type, for example when concatenating with plus or comparing with the double equals operator. The abstract operations behind this are ToString, ToNumber, ToBoolean and ToPrimitive, and knowing their order resolves the puzzles that make JavaScript notorious.

The plus operator is overloaded: if either operand is a string it concatenates, otherwise it adds numerically. That is why one plus one is two but one plus the string one is the string eleven. The boolean conversion is simple: false, zero, negative zero, empty string, null, undefined and not-a-number are falsy, and everything else is truthy, including empty arrays and empty objects. Prefer explicit conversion at boundaries so the reader never has to simulate the rules.

### Equality and identity

The double equals operator compares after coercion, and the triple equals operator compares without conversion. The strict operator returns true only for values of the same type that are equal, with the special rule that not-a-number is not equal to itself. The loose operator follows a conversion algorithm that makes expressions such as zero equals empty string true and null equals undefined true, which is rarely what you want.

Use triple equals almost everywhere so comparisons are predictable. The one idiomatic use of loose equality is the null check, where value equals null is true for both null and undefined and is a compact way to test for either. Object comparison always compares references, so two distinct objects that look identical are not equal; comparing by value requires comparing the fields you care about or using a dedicated equality helper.

Numbers are double-precision binary floating point following the IEEE 754 standard, which gives 53 bits of integer precision and introduces representation error for fractions that are not powers of two. That is why zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three. Comparisons of floating point results should use a tolerance, and money should be handled in integer minor units or a decimal library rather than in floats.

The safe integer range is the numbers between the negative and positive value of two to the fifty-third power minus one, exposed as Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and its negative counterpart. Beyond that range, distinct integers may map to the same value. Number.isSafeInteger tests membership in the range, and Number.isFinite distinguishes real numbers from the special values infinity and not-a-number. Because not-a-number is the only value unequal to itself, Number.isNaN is the reliable test, unlike the global isNaN which coerces its argument first.

### Code

Parsing and validating are different jobs. `Number` is strict; `parseInt` stops at the first bad character:

```js
console.log(Number(''));          // 0      <- the empty-string trap
console.log(Number('12px'));      // NaN
console.log(parseInt('12px', 10)); // 12
console.log(Number('0x1f'));      // 31
console.log(Number(null), Number(undefined));  // 0 NaN
```

The safe integer boundary is where ids start colliding:

```js
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);            // 9007199254740991
console.log(9007199254740993 === 9007199254740992);  // true — both rounded
console.log(BigInt('9007199254740993') + 1n);    // 9007199254740994n
```

Rounding and formatting behave differently, and `toFixed` is not a rounding function:

```js
console.log((1.005).toFixed(2));     // '1.00' — 1.005 is stored just below
console.log(Math.round(-0.5));       // -0
console.log(Math.trunc(-2.7), Math.floor(-2.7));   // -2 -3
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.5));
// '1.234,50 €'
```

### BigInt, rounding and parsing

BigInt represents arbitrarily large integers exactly and is written with a trailing n, such as nine hundred quintillion n. BigInt and number cannot be mixed in arithmetic without an explicit conversion, because doing so could silently lose precision. Use BigInt for identifiers, cryptography and counters that exceed the safe integer range, and numbers for ordinary arithmetic. Comparisons between BigInt and number work, but addition and multiplication do not.

Rounding is available through Math.round, Math.floor, Math.ceil and Math.trunc, and formatting through toFixed and Intl.NumberFormat. Parsing integers and floats uses parseInt and parseFloat, which stop at the first invalid character and therefore silently accept trailing junk; Number is stricter and returns not-a-number for anything that is not a full numeric literal. For user input, prefer Number with an explicit validity check, or parse with a validating regular expression.

### Randomness and the Math object

The Math object provides constants such as Math.PI and functions for trigonometry, exponentiation, logarithms, absolute value, minimum and maximum, and rounding. Math.random returns a pseudo-random number in the half-open interval from zero inclusive to one exclusive. A random integer in a range is built by multiplying by the span and flooring, being careful to add the lower bound and to use the exclusive upper bound correctly.

Math.random is not cryptographically secure. For tokens, passwords or anything with a security implication, use the random values API provided by the host, such as the web crypto getRandomValues method. Seeding is not supported, so tests that depend on randomness should inject a random function rather than patch Math.random, which keeps tests deterministic and the production code untouched.

A string is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units. Methods such as slice, substring, replace, toUpperCase, trim, split, padStart and includes return new strings rather than modifying the original. Indexing with square brackets returns a single code unit as a string, and length counts code units, not characters, which matters for characters outside the basic multilingual plane such as many emoji, which occupy two code units.

Because strings are immutable they can be safely shared and used as map keys. Building large strings by repeated concatenation is acceptable in modern engines, but joining an array of parts with join is clearer for lists. Template literals add interpolation and multi-line text and are the modern default for anything containing a value, while plain quotes remain fine for fixed text.

### Code

Strings are immutable, so every method returns a new one. The position methods differ in ways worth memorising:

```js
const s = '  Hello, World!  ';
console.log(s.trim());                 // 'Hello, World!'
console.log(s.slice(2, 7));            // 'Hello'
console.log(s.slice(-4, -2));          // 'd!'
console.log(s.substring(7, 2));        // 'Hello' — arguments swap!
console.log('a-b-c'.split('-').length);        // 3
console.log('a-b-c'.replace('-', '+'));        // 'a+b-c'  first only
console.log('a-b-c'.replaceAll('-', '+'));     // 'a+b+c'
```

Template literals are the readable way to build text, and tagged templates let you process it before it becomes a string:

```js
const user = { name: 'Ana', role: 'admin' };
console.log(`${user.name} (${user.role})`);    // Ana (admin)

function upper(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((out, part, i) => out + part + (values[i] ?? '').toString().toUpperCase(), '');
}
console.log(upper`hello ${user.name}`);        // hello ANA
```

Code units versus code points matters as soon as non-ASCII text appears:

```js
console.log('😀'.length);              // 2
console.log([...'😀'].length);         // 1
console.log('é'.normalize('NFC').length, 'e\u0301'.normalize('NFD').length);   // 1 2
console.log('e\u0301'.normalize('NFD').replace(/\p{M}/gu, ''));                // 'e'
```

### Template literals

Template literals are delimited by backticks and support interpolation with a dollar sign and braces, plus multi-line content without escape sequences. Tagged templates pass the literal parts and the interpolated values separately to a function, enabling domain-specific languages such as styled components or safe query builders. This is the mechanism behind several popular libraries and is part of the core language rather than an extension.

Because interpolation is automatic string conversion, prefer template literals over concatenation for readability and to avoid precedence mistakes. Be careful with untrusted values: interpolating user text into HTML or SQL is an injection risk. Template literals do not escape anything, so escaping must be done by a dedicated function or by using a library that understands the target syntax.

### Unicode and internationalisation

Strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, so a character outside the basic plane is a surrogate pair of two code units. Iterating a string with a for-of loop or using Array.from yields code points rather than code units and therefore handles emoji correctly. The normalise method converts between canonical Unicode forms, which matters when comparing visually identical text that was composed differently.

Locale-aware comparison and formatting come from Intl rather than from simple operators. Intl.Collator sorts strings according to a locale's rules, where accented letters sort near their base letters, and Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.DateTimeFormat and Intl.ListFormat produce localised output. Using these avoids hand-rolled formatting and keeps text correct across languages and regions.

The boolean type has exactly two values, true and false. Logical operators and conditions convert their operands using the truthy and falsy rules, and the conversion is not limited to booleans: the logical and operator returns the first falsy operand or the last operand, and the logical or returns the first truthy operand or the last. This short-circuit behaviour is used to supply defaults and to guard dereferences.

The nullish coalescing operator is a stricter default: it returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined, unlike the logical or which also replaces other falsy values such as zero and the empty string. Choosing between them is a common source of bugs. Use the logical or for presence checks on objects and the nullish operator when zero or the empty string is a legitimate value.

### Code

`??` and `||` are not interchangeable: `||` falls through on every falsy value, `??` only on null and undefined:

```js
const config = { retries: 0, label: '' };
console.log(config.retries || 3);    // 3   <- wrong, 0 was a real value
console.log(config.retries ?? 3);    // 0
console.log(config.label || 'none'); // 'none'
console.log(config.label ?? 'none'); // ''
```

The same distinction applies to default parameters and to destructuring:

```js
function connect({ timeout = 5000, retries = 0 } = {}) {
  return { timeout, retries };
}
console.log(connect());                       // { timeout: 5000, retries: 0 }
console.log(connect({ timeout: 0 }));         // { timeout: 0, retries: 0 }
console.log(connect({ timeout: null }));      // { timeout: null, retries: 0 }
```

A `Symbol` is a guaranteed-unique key, which makes it the right tool for metadata that must not collide:

```js
const HIDDEN = Symbol('hidden');
const row = { id: 1, [HIDDEN]: 'internal' };
console.log(Object.keys(row));            // [ 'id' ]
console.log(row[HIDDEN]);                  // 'internal'
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(row).length);  // 1
```

### null, undefined and absence

undefined means a value was never assigned, and is what a missing property, a missing argument and an uninitialised var all produce. null is an explicit absence that a programmer sets on purpose. Both are falsy and both loosely equal each other but not anything else. Treating the two as different signals, and defaulting to undefined for unset values, keeps intent clear.

Optional chaining short-circuits property access when a value is null or undefined, turning a crash into undefined. Combined with the nullish coalescing operator it expresses defaults cleanly: read configuration property with a fallback in one expression. Do not use optional chaining everywhere, because it can hide a genuine programming error; use it at real boundaries such as optional configuration or responses from external systems.

### Symbols

A symbol is a unique, immutable primitive often used as a property key that cannot collide with string keys. Two symbols with the same description are different values. Symbols are skipped by ordinary property enumeration and JSON serialisation, which makes them useful for attaching metadata without polluting the visible shape of an object. The global symbol registry, reached through Symbol.for and Symbol.keyFor, lets different parts of a program share a symbol by name.

Well-known symbols customise language behaviour: Symbol.iterator makes an object iterable, Symbol.asyncIterator does the same for async iteration, Symbol.toPrimitive controls coercion, and Symbol.hasInstance customises the instanceof operator. Implementing these hooks is how user types cooperate with for-of, spread, destructuring and other built-in machinery.

An object is a collection of key-value pairs where keys are strings or symbols and values are any type. Literal syntax uses braces with colon-separated pairs, commas between them, shorthand for variables of the same name, computed keys in square brackets, and method shorthand. Properties are read with dot notation for fixed names and bracket notation for dynamic names or names that are not valid identifiers.

Reading a missing property yields undefined rather than throwing, which is convenient but hides mistakes; deleting a property with the delete operator removes it and can hurt performance because it changes the object's hidden shape. Prefer setting a property to undefined or restructuring the data over deleting keys in hot paths. Checking for existence is done with the in operator or hasOwnProperty, which behave differently for inherited properties.

### Code

Object literals do more than list key-value pairs:

```js
const key = 'role';
const name = 'Ana';
const user = {
  name,                          // shorthand
  [key]: 'admin',                // computed key
  greet() { return `hi ${this.name}`; },   // method shorthand
  ['a' + 'b']: 1,
};
console.log(user, user.greet());
```

Reading safely, copying shallowly, and iterating are the three operations you use constantly:

```js
const settings = { theme: 'dark', nested: { size: 2 } };
console.log(settings?.nested?.size);        // 2
console.log('theme' in settings);           // true
console.log(Object.hasOwn(settings, 'theme'));   // true, ignores the prototype

const copy = { ...settings };
copy.nested.size = 9;
console.log(settings.nested.size);          // 9 — shallow!
console.log(Object.entries(settings));      // [ ['theme','dark'], ['nested',{size:9}] ]
```

The prototype chain is why `in` and `hasOwnProperty` disagree:

```js
const o = { a: 1 };
console.log('toString' in o);                     // true — inherited
console.log(Object.hasOwn(o, 'toString'));        // false
console.log(Object.keys(o));                      // [ 'a' ] — own, enumerable only
```

### Copying, merging and freezing

Object.assign copies own enumerable properties from sources into a target, and the spread syntax in an object literal produces a shallow copy. Both are shallow, so nested objects are still shared with the original. A deep copy that handles nested data is available as structuredClone for cloneable values, while JSON round-tripping works only for JSON-safe data and silently drops functions, undefined and symbols.

Object.freeze prevents adding, removing or changing properties and is shallow, so nested objects must be frozen individually or by a recursive helper. Object.seal prevents adding and removing but allows changing values. Immutability aids reasoning but freezing every object has a cost, so apply it at boundaries where a shared value must not change, such as a configuration object.

### Iterating keys, values and entries

Object.keys, Object.values and Object.entries return arrays of the own enumerable string keys, values or pairs, which are convenient for mapping and destructuring. The for-in loop visits enumerable properties including inherited ones, so it should be guarded with hasOwnProperty or replaced by Object.entries, which is predictable and produces both the key and the value.

Property order is defined: integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols. Rely on this only when it is part of the specification; do not depend on insertion order for keys that look like indices. When order matters and the data is not object-shaped, prefer a Map, which preserves insertion order for every key type and has a size property.

Arithmetic operators include plus, minus, multiply, divide, modulo and exponent. The increment and decrement operators change a variable by one and exist in prefix and postfix forms that differ in the value they yield. Compound assignment operators such as plus-equals combine an operation with assignment. Comparison operators include the ordered relations, which coerce to numbers then to strings, and the equality operators discussed elsewhere.

Operator precedence determines grouping, and associativity determines the order for operators of equal precedence. Rather than memorising the full table, use parentheses whenever the intent is not obvious. The comma operator evaluates its left operand, discards it, and yields the right; it is rarely needed outside for-loop headers and is best avoided in ordinary expressions.

### Code

The logical assignment operators only write when they need to, which matters for setters and for `localStorage`-style side effects:

```js
const state = { count: 0, name: '' };
state.count ||= 5;      // 0 is falsy  -> becomes 5
state.name ??= 'anon';  // '' is not nullish -> stays ''
state.missing ??= 1;    // becomes 1
console.log(state);     // { count: 5, name: '', missing: 1 }
```

Short-circuiting is also how you guard a call:

```js
const cache = new Map();
const get = (k) => cache.get(k);

cache.set('a', 0);
console.log(get('a') ?? 'missing');     // 0
console.log(get('b') ?? 'missing');     // 'missing'

const obj = { fn: () => 'ran' };
console.log(obj.fn?.());                // 'ran'
console.log(obj.missing?.());           // undefined, not a TypeError
```

The comma operator and the conditional operator are both expressions, so they can appear where a value is expected:

```js
const grade = (score) => score >= 90 ? 'A' : score >= 80 ? 'B' : 'C';
console.log([95, 85, 70].map(grade));    // [ 'A', 'B', 'C' ]

let a = 0;
const b = (a += 1, a * 10);
console.log(a, b);                       // 1 10
```

### Logical, nullish and bitwise operators

The logical operators and, or and not short-circuit and return one of their operands. The nullish coalescing operator supplies a default only for null and undefined. Logical assignment operators combine these with assignment, for example or-equals and nullish-equals, which are handy for lazy initialisation. These operators return values, not forced booleans, so they can build expressions rather than just conditions.

Bitwise operators treat their operands as thirty-two-bit signed integers and include and, or, xor, not, shifts and unsigned shift. They are used for flags, hashing tricks and performance-sensitive code. Because they truncate to thirty-two bits they silently corrupt larger numbers, so they should never be applied to values that can exceed that range. Double bitwise not is a known trick for truncating to an integer, but Math.trunc is clearer and safer.

### Conditional, spread and optional chaining

The conditional operator, often called the ternary operator, chooses between two expressions based on a condition and is the only operator with three operands. It is an expression, so it can appear inside other expressions, which is useful for a value that depends on a condition. Nested ternaries quickly become unreadable and should be replaced by a lookup or an if statement.

The spread operator expands an iterable into a function call or array literal and spreads object properties into an object literal, while the rest pattern collects remaining items into an array or object. Optional chaining guards property access and calls, and combines with nullish coalescing for defaults. Together these operators make modern data manipulation concise, but each should be used where it clarifies intent rather than to save keystrokes.

The value of this depends on how a function is called. As a method it is the receiver object; as a plain call in strict mode it is undefined and in sloppy mode the global object; as a constructor with new it is the newly created object; and inside an arrow function it is inherited from the enclosing lexical scope. The call site decides, not the definition, except for arrows which have no this of their own.

Because this is determined at call time, extracting a method and calling it separately loses its receiver, which is why passing an object's method as a callback often fails with an undefined property error. The fixes are to bind the method, wrap it in an arrow, or capture the receiver in a variable. Modern style favours arrow functions inside methods so callbacks keep the method's this.

### Code

`this` is decided by how a function is called, not where it was defined — except for arrow functions, which inherit it:

```js
const obj = {
  name: 'obj',
  regular() { return this?.name; },
  arrow: () => typeof window !== 'undefined' ? 'window' : 'module',
};
console.log(obj.regular());                 // 'obj'
const loose = obj.regular;
console.log(loose());                       // undefined — called with no receiver
console.log(loose.call(obj));               // 'obj'
console.log(loose.apply(obj, []));          // 'obj'
const bound = loose.bind(obj);
console.log(bound());                       // 'obj'
```

`bind` returns a new function; `call` and `apply` invoke immediately and differ only in how arguments are passed:

```js
function describe(prefix, suffix) {
  return `${prefix}${this.name}${suffix}`;
}
const user = { name: 'Ana' };
console.log(describe.call(user, '[', ']'));      // [Ana]
console.log(describe.apply(user, ['{', '}']));   // {Ana}
console.log(describe.bind(user)('(', ')'));      // (Ana)
```

The practical rule: use arrow functions for callbacks so you keep the surrounding `this`, and use method shorthand for anything that needs the receiver.

### call, apply and bind

The call and apply methods invoke a function with an explicitly chosen this, differing only in how arguments are passed: call takes them individually and apply takes an array. The bind method returns a new function permanently bound to a given this and optional preset arguments, enabling partial application. These methods make function borrowing possible, such as applying array methods to array-like objects.

Borrowing is now less necessary because spread converts array-like values to arrays. Bind is still valuable for event handlers and for callbacks that will be invoked later without a receiver. Remember that binding creates a new function, so binding the same method repeatedly in a hot path allocates unnecessarily; bind once and reuse the result.

### Classes, methods and this in practice

Class methods are strict and have this bound to the instance when called normally. A common bug is passing an instance method as a callback, where this becomes undefined. Solutions include an arrow class field that captures the instance, binding in the constructor, or calling the method through an arrow at the use site. Class fields declared with an arrow turn the method into an instance property that is already bound.

Do not assume this is always an object. In strict mode plain calls produce undefined, and frameworks sometimes call functions with a chosen receiver. When a function does not need a receiver, write it as a standalone function or an arrow so this is irrelevant, which removes a whole class of bugs and makes the function easier to reuse.

Every object has an internal link to another object called its prototype, reachable through Object.getPrototypeOf and settable at creation with Object.create. When a property is read and not found on the object itself, the engine follows the prototype link and repeats, forming the prototype chain, until it reaches the end where the prototype is null. This is how methods are shared: they live on the prototype and every instance reaches them through the chain.

Functions have a prototype property used when they act as constructors, and Object.prototype sits at the top of most chains, providing methods such as hasOwnProperty and toString. Inheritance in JavaScript is therefore delegation: an object does not copy its parent's members, it looks them up live. Changing a prototype method affects all instances at once, which is powerful and also a reason to treat prototypes as shared and stable.

### Code

Every object has an internal link to a prototype, and a missing property lookup walks that chain:

```js
const base = { greet() { return `hi ${this.name}`; } };
const user = Object.create(base);
user.name = 'Ana';

console.log(user.greet());                       // 'hi Ana'
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(user) === base);   // true
console.log(user.hasOwnProperty('greet'));       // false — inherited
console.log('name' in user);                     // true
```

`new` does four things, and knowing them removes the magic:

```js
function Person(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
Person.prototype.greet = function () { return `hi ${this.name}`; };

const p = new Person('Bo');
console.log(p.greet());                          // 'hi Bo'
console.log(p.constructor === Person);           // true
console.log(p instanceof Person);                // true
console.log(Person.prototype.isPrototypeOf(p));  // true
```

A null prototype is the safe container for data you did not create:

```js
const dict = Object.create(null);
dict['__proto__'] = 'a real key now';
console.log(Object.keys(dict));          // [ '__proto__' ]
console.log(typeof dict.toString);       // 'undefined' — no inherited methods
const normal = {};
normal['__proto__'] = 'ignored';
console.log(Object.keys(normal));        // []
```

### Creating and wiring prototypes

Object.create makes a new object with a chosen prototype and is the cleanest way to express pure delegation, optionally defining own properties in one call. Linking a derived constructor's prototype is done by assigning Object.create of the base prototype and resetting the constructor property so the reference is accurate. Without that reset, the constructor property points at the base, which confuses introspection code.

Shallow copying with spread or Object.assign copies own enumerable properties and does not copy the prototype, so the copy loses inherited methods. Use Object.create or a class when you want to preserve behaviour, and shallow copies when you want a plain data object. The getPrototypeOf and setPrototypeOf functions allow inspection and reassignment, but changing a prototype at runtime deoptimises objects and should be avoided in hot paths.

### instanceof and property lookup

The instanceof operator walks the prototype chain of the left operand looking for the prototype of the right operand, so it answers whether an object was built from a constructor anywhere in its lineage. Because it depends on the prototype link it can be fooled by objects created with Object.create from the same prototype, which is usually desirable and occasionally surprising. A custom Symbol.hasInstance method can override the behaviour.

The in operator reports whether a property exists anywhere in the chain, while hasOwnProperty reports only own properties. Distinguishing the two matters when iterating or validating objects: inherited methods would otherwise count as data. Use Object.hasOwn, the modern static form, because it is safe even on objects that override hasOwnProperty or have no prototype at all.

Every property has attributes: value, writable, enumerable and configurable. Object.defineProperty sets them explicitly and is how non-writable constants and non-enumerable internal properties are created. Getters and setters are expressed as an accessor descriptor with get and set functions instead of a value. Enumerability controls whether a property shows up in for-in and Object.keys, which is how built-in prototypes keep their methods out of the way.

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor reads the attributes back, and Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors gathers them for many properties at once, which is the correct way to copy an object including getters and non-enumerable keys. Using these utilities is uncommon in application code but essential when building libraries that need to control exactly how properties behave.

### Code

Descriptors control writability, enumerability and configurability, which is how you build read-only or hidden properties:

```js
const config = {};
Object.defineProperty(config, 'version', {
  value: 2,
  writable: false,
  enumerable: false,
  configurable: false,
});
console.log(config.version);            // 2
console.log(Object.keys(config));       // [] — non-enumerable
config.version = 9;
console.log(config.version);            // 2 — silent failure in sloppy mode
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(config, 'version').writable);   // false
```

Getters and setters look like fields but run code:

```js
const temp = {
  _c: 0,
  get celsius() { return this._c; },
  set celsius(v) { this._c = Number(v); },
  get fahrenheit() { return this._c * 1.8 + 32; },
};
temp.celsius = '25';
console.log(temp.celsius, temp.fahrenheit);   // 25 77
```

Freezing and sealing are different strengths of immutability, and both are shallow:

```js
const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } });
frozen.a = 2;              // ignored in sloppy mode, throws in strict mode
frozen.nested.b = 3;       // allowed — the nested object is not frozen
console.log(frozen.a, frozen.nested.b);       // 1 3
console.log(Object.isFrozen(frozen));         // true
```

### Freezing, sealing and ownership

Object.freeze makes an object and its properties non-writable and non-configurable, Object.seal prevents adding and removing but allows writing, and Object.preventExtensions only blocks new properties. All three are shallow, so a frozen object can still contain a mutable array. A recursive deep freeze helper is straightforward but must guard against cycles by tracking visited objects.

Ownership questions are answered by a family of predicates: isExtensible, isFrozen and isSealed report the current state. Freezing configuration and shared constants prevents accidental mutation across modules and turns a silent bug into a thrown error in strict mode. Because freezing has a runtime cost and blocks later extension, apply it deliberately to values that should never change rather than to every object.

### Comparison, cloning and serialisation

There is no built-in deep equality for objects, so two structurally identical objects are not equal. Common approaches are to compare the fields that matter, to use JSON serialisation when the data is JSON-safe, or to use a structural equality utility. Each has limits: JSON comparison ignores key order but drops undefined, functions and symbols, and it fails on cyclic structures.

structuredClone performs a real deep clone and handles nested objects, arrays, maps, sets and typed arrays, but it cannot clone functions, DOM nodes or class prototypes. JSON.stringify is for serialisation rather than cloning and supports a replacer and indentation. A custom toJSON method on an object controls how it is serialised, which is how Date, Map and Set produce sensible JSON representations.

An array is an ordered list of values with a numeric length. Literal syntax uses square brackets, and Array.from converts iterables or array-like values into real arrays, with an optional mapping function. The spread operator copies elements into a new array. Push and pop work at the end, shift and unshift at the beginning, splice removes and inserts in the middle, and slice copies a range without mutating.

Mutating methods change the receiver and are the source of subtle bugs when an array is shared. Prefer non-mutating methods for data transformation and reserve mutation for genuinely local arrays. Sparse arrays, created by assigning past the current length or by the array constructor with a single number, behave inconsistently across methods because empty slots are skipped by some and treated as undefined by others.

### Code

The three that do most of the work, and the fact that they do not mutate:

```js
const orders = [
  { id: 1, total: 120, paid: true },
  { id: 2, total: 40, paid: false },
  { id: 3, total: 75, paid: true },
];

const paidTotal = orders
  .filter((o) => o.paid)
  .map((o) => o.total)
  .reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
console.log(paidTotal);                        // 195
console.log(orders.length);                    // 3 — untouched
```

Mutating methods are the other half, and mixing the two kinds up is the usual bug:

```js
const xs = [3, 1, 2];
xs.sort((a, b) => a - b);          // mutates
console.log(xs);                   // [1, 2, 3]
console.log([10, 9, 80].sort());   // [10, 80, 9] — lexicographic!
console.log([10, 9, 80].sort((a, b) => a - b));   // [9, 10, 80]

const ys = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(ys.splice(1, 1), ys);  // [2] [1, 3]  — splice mutates
console.log(ys.toSpliced(1, 1));   // [1] — the copying version
```

Searching, flattening and the modern accessors:

```js
const users = [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }];
console.log(users.find((u) => u.id === 2));        // { id: 2 }
console.log(users.findIndex((u) => u.id === 2));   // 1
console.log(users.some((u) => u.id > 1));          // true
console.log(users.every((u) => u.id > 0));         // true
console.log([1, [2, [3]]].flat(2));                // [1, 2, 3]
console.log([1, 2].flatMap((n) => [n, n * 10]));   // [1, 10, 2, 20]
console.log([1, 2, 3].at(-1));                     // 3
```

### map, filter, reduce and friends

The transforming methods are the everyday tools of array work. map produces a new array with each element transformed, filter keeps elements satisfying a predicate, find and findIndex locate the first match, some and every test whole-array conditions, and includes tests membership. flat and flatMap flatten nested arrays one level or while mapping, and sort orders in place using a comparator that must return a negative, zero or positive number.

reduce folds an array into a single value by calling a reducer with an accumulator and the current element. It can express sums, grouping, and building objects, but it is also easy to write an unreadable reduce; a clear loop or a specialised method is often better. Always supply an initial accumulator so an empty array does not throw, and remember that sort mutates, so copy first with spread when the original order matters.

### Iteration order, copying and length

Arrays preserve insertion order, which makes them the right structure when order is meaningful and keys are positional. Copying is shallow: the spread operator, slice, and Array.from all produce a new array whose elements are the same references, so nested objects are still shared. A deep copy requires structuredClone or an explicit recursive routine.

The length property is writable: setting it smaller truncates the array, and larger creates empty slots. Using length as a delete is a trap, so remove elements with splice, filter or pop instead. The array methods that accept callbacks pass the element, the index and the whole array, which is occasionally useful but more often a source of confusion when the callback signature is mistaken.

An ArrayBuffer is a fixed-length block of raw bytes with no notion of values. A typed array view, such as Uint8Array or Float64Array, interprets that memory as a sequence of numbers of a fixed width. Creating a typed array allocates a buffer automatically, and several views can share one buffer, which is how binary formats are decoded and how the same bytes are read as different numeric types.

Unlike ordinary arrays, typed arrays have a fixed length, hold only numbers, and do not change shape, which makes them fast and predictable. They also do not participate in the same optimisations as normal arrays for object elements. DataView provides explicit endianness control and is used when parsing formats whose byte order is defined, such as network protocols and file headers.

### Code

A typed array is a view over a fixed-size buffer, and the byte order is the platform's:

```js
const bytes = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 255]);
console.log(bytes.length, bytes.byteLength);     // 3 3
console.log(bytes.at(-1));                       // 255
bytes[0] = 300;                                  // truncates, no error
console.log(bytes[0]);                           // 44
console.log(bytes.toString());                   // '1,2,255'

const f64 = new Float64Array([1.5, 2.5]);
console.log(f64.length, f64.byteLength);         // 2 16
```

`DataView` is the explicit-endianness reader you need for a binary protocol:

```js
const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8);
const view = new DataView(buf);
view.setUint32(0, 0x01020304, false);            // big-endian
console.log(view.getUint8(0).toString(16));      // '1'
console.log(view.getUint32(0, false).toString(16));  // '1020304'
view.setFloat32(4, 1.5, true);                   // little-endian
console.log(view.getFloat32(4, true));           // 1.5
```

Text and bytes convert through the encoder classes, and chunk boundaries are where hand-rolled code breaks:

```js
const encoder = new TextEncoder();
const decoder = new TextDecoder('utf-8');
console.log(encoder.encode('héllo').length);     // 6 bytes, not 5 chars
console.log(decoder.decode(encoder.encode('héllo')));   // 'héllo'

const binary = new TextDecoder('utf-8', { fatal: true });
try { binary.decode(new Uint8Array([0xff, 0xfe])); }
catch (err) { console.log(err.name); }           // TypeError
console.log(decoder.decode(new Uint8Array([0xff, 0xfe])));   // '��' — silent replacement
```

### Text encoding and binary conversion

TextEncoder converts a string to UTF-8 bytes and TextDecoder does the reverse, both operating over typed arrays and buffers. This is the standard way to move between strings and binary data in browsers and in modern Node, replacing ad-hoc routines. Base64 conversion uses the host's btoa and atob functions or, in Node, the Buffer type's toString with a base64 encoding.

Binary blobs from files, fetch responses and canvas are represented by ArrayBuffer, Blob and typed arrays, and conversions between them are routine. A Blob is a file-like immutable object that can be read as text, array buffer or stream; a Response can be turned into any of these. Knowing which representation an API returns, and which it expects, avoids unnecessary copies of large data.

### When binary handling matters

Binary handling appears whenever performance or interoperability with external systems is involved: image and audio processing, cryptography, compression, network protocols, and WebAssembly memory. WebAssembly shares memory with JavaScript through an ArrayBuffer, so typed arrays are the bridge between the two. Cryptographic operations from the web crypto API also take and return buffers.

If your work is ordinary application logic, plain strings, numbers and JSON will cover it, and binary types can be ignored. Reach for typed arrays when a profiler shows that string or object manipulation dominates, when a protocol or file format demands exact bytes, or when integrating with native code. Otherwise, clarity wins over byte-level control.

A regular expression is a pattern for matching text, written as a literal between slashes or built with the RegExp constructor for dynamic patterns. Flags modify behaviour: global finds all matches, ignore-case matches case-insensitively, multiline makes anchors match line boundaries, dot-all lets the dot match newlines, unicode enables full code point semantics, and sticky anchors matches at the last index. Patterns support character classes, quantifiers, groups, alternation, anchors and backreferences.

The test method reports whether a pattern matches, exec returns a match object with captured groups and position, and string methods such as match, matchAll, replace, search and split use regular expressions too. When replace is given a function, the function computes each replacement using the matched text and groups, which enables complex transformations. Named capture groups make replacements readable by referring to group names instead of positions.

### Code

The difference between `match`, `matchAll` and `exec` trips everyone up:

```js
const text = 'a1 b2 c3';
console.log(text.match(/[a-z]/));         // first match only, with .index
console.log(text.match(/[a-z]/g));        // all matches, no index
console.log([...text.matchAll(/([a-z])(\d)/g)].map((m) => m[2]));   // [ '1', '2', '3' ]
```

Named groups and the replacement function are clearer than numbered captures:

```js
const date = '2024-03-17';
const m = /(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})/.exec(date);
console.log(m.groups);                    // { y: '2024', m: '03', d: '17' }

const csv = '1,2,3';
console.log(csv.replace(/(\d)/g, (match, digit) => String(Number(digit) * 2)));   // '2,4,6'
console.log(csv.replace(/(\d)/g, '$1$1'));   // '11,22,33'
console.log('a.b'.replace(/[.]/g, '-'));     // 'a-b' — escape the dot!
```

A global regex carries `lastIndex`, so reusing one on two strings silently skips matches:

```js
const g = /\d/g;
g.exec('12');
console.log(g.lastIndex);        // 1
console.log(g.test('34'));       // true, but starts from index 1

// safe: create a fresh regex per call, or use matchAll / match with g
const count = (s) => [...s.matchAll(/\d/g)].length;
console.log(count('12'), count('34'));   // 2 2
```

### Writing safe patterns

Regular expressions can be catastrophically slow. A pattern with nested quantifiers over overlapping alternatives can backtrack exponentially on crafted input, freezing the process, a problem known as catastrophic backtracking. Avoiding ambiguous repetition, anchoring patterns, and preferring linear constructs prevents it. When a pattern is applied to untrusted input with a time budget, validate with a simpler rule first or use a library that guarantees linear time.

Always anchor a pattern when the whole string must match, using start and end anchors, because an unanchored pattern matches a substring and silently accepts invalid input. Escape literal characters that have meaning in a pattern using the escape function or a helper. Regular expressions are excellent for validation of simple formats and poor for parsing nested structures such as HTML or balanced parentheses, which call for a real parser.

### Practical uses

Regular expressions shine at tokenising, simple validation such as email shape or version strings, extracting fields from log lines, and bulk text transformation. They are also the basis of the string replace and split methods, including splitting on multiple delimiters. Keep patterns small and named, and add a comment when the intent is obscure, because a dense pattern is unreadable a week later.

For structured data, prefer a parser over a pattern. JSON, HTML, CSV with quoted fields and programming languages all have grammars that regular expressions cannot fully capture; a tokenizer plus parser, or an existing library, is the correct tool. Using a pattern for such formats usually works on the easy cases and fails on the hard ones, which is the worst combination for reliability.

sections.title: Single thread and the task queue
The Date object and its hazards

pages.text:
Hoisting is the registration of declarations before execution. The temporal dead zone is the period before a let or const binding is initialised. A closure is a function together with the bindings it captured. The prototype chain is the sequence of prototypes consulted during property lookup. A microtask is a callback run after the current task and before the next, and a task is a unit of work taken from the event loop queue.

A promise is a placeholder for a future value; thenable is any object with a then method. A stream delivers data in chunks with backpressure. Tree shaking removes unused exports during bundling. A polyfill implements a missing built-in, while a transpiler rewrites syntax. Idempotent means an operation can be repeated with the same effect. Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer slows a fast producer.

### Code

Operator precedence, in the order that actually matters when reading code:

```js
// member . [] ()  then unary ! typeof ++ --  then **  then * / %
// then + -  then < > <= >= in instanceof  then == != === !==
// then &&  then || ??  then ?:  then = += ...  then ,
console.log(2 + 3 * 4);          // 14
console.log((2 + 3) * 4);        // 20
console.log(2 ** 3 ** 2);        // 512 — right-associative
console.log(!0 + 1);             // 2 — ! binds tighter than +
console.log(1 < 2 < 3);          // true  ((1<2) -> true -> 1 < 3)
console.log(3 > 2 > 1);          // false ((3>2) -> true -> 1 > 1)
```

Falsy values, equality, and the one loose comparison worth keeping:

```js
// falsy: false 0 -0 0n '' null undefined NaN
typeof undefined        // 'undefined'
typeof null             // 'object'  (the historical bug)
Object.is(NaN, NaN)     // true
Object.is(0, -0)        // false
value == null           // true for both null and undefined, false for 0 and ''
```

Array and object recipes worth having at hand:

```js
const clone = structuredClone(obj);
const merged = { ...a, ...b };
const without = (({ id, ...rest }) => rest)(row);
const byId = Object.fromEntries(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
const unique = [...new Set(list)];
const sorted = [...list].sort((a, b) => a - b);       // copy first
const last = list.at(-1);
const grouped = Object.groupBy(rows, (r) => r.type);    // ES2024
const sum = list.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
const range = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i);   // [0,1,2,3,4]
const shuffled = list.toSorted(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
```

### Quick reference

Declare with const by default and let when reassignment is needed. Convert to a number explicitly with Number and validate; compare with triple equals except for the null check. Use the nullish coalescing operator for defaults when zero or empty string are valid. Build strings with template literals, transform arrays with map and filter, and model keyed lookup with a Map when keys are dynamic.

Run asynchronous work with async and await, parallelise independent calls with Promise.all, and cancel with an AbortController. Catch errors at the boundary that can act on them and rethrow the rest. Store timestamps in UTC and format with Intl. Prefer textContent over innerHTML with untrusted data. Measure before optimising, and remove listeners and timers when a component is disposed.

### Going further

The authoritative reference is the ECMAScript specification, which defines exact behaviour, and the MDN documentation, which explains it for practitioners with examples and compatibility tables. Reading the specification is worthwhile when behaviour is surprising, such as coercion order or the precise semantics of equality.

Beyond the language, the ecosystem is built from a small set of durable ideas: modules, the event loop, promises, the prototype model and the standard library. Mastering those ideas transfers across frameworks and runtimes, whereas framework-specific knowledge dates quickly. The most reliable way to deepen understanding is to build something small without a framework, then read the source of a library that solves the same problem well.

sections.title: Reading coercion like the engine does

pages.text:
The abstract operation ToPrimitive is what every surprising coercion goes through. When an object meets an operator that needs a primitive, the engine calls Symbol.toPrimitive if present, otherwise valueOf, otherwise toString, using the hint number, string or default. Arrays have a toString that joins with commas, which is why [1, 2] + [3, 4] evaluates to the string 1,23,4: both sides become strings and the plus concatenates them. An empty array becomes the empty string, so [] + [] is the empty string and [] + {} is the string [object Object].

The classic puzzle {} + [] deserves its own explanation. At the start of a statement the braces are parsed as an empty block, so the expression is the unary plus applied to an empty array, which converts to the number zero. Wrap the same text in parentheses and it becomes an object plus an array, producing the string [object Object]. This is proof that the parse position changes behaviour, and a good reason never to start a statement with a brace or bracket.

The number conversions follow a documented table. undefined becomes NaN, null becomes zero, an empty string becomes zero, a whitespace-only string becomes zero, and a non-numeric string becomes NaN. The boolean conversions are a fixed list of falsy values: false, zero, negative zero, the empty string, NaN, null and undefined. Everything else, including empty arrays, empty objects and the string zero, is truthy.

A practical debugging technique is to ask what type each operand actually is before the operator runs. Printing typeof and the value at the boundary usually explains the surprise immediately. When a comparison produces a result you cannot explain, rewrite both sides as explicit Number or String conversions and the behaviour becomes predictable.

### Code

The equality table, abridged to the rows that surprise people:

```js
console.log(null == undefined);     // true
console.log(null == 0);             // false
console.log('' == 0);               // true
console.log(' \t' == 0);            // true
console.log([] == false);           // true
console.log([] == '');              // true
console.log([0] == false);          // true   ([0] -> '0' -> 0)
console.log({} == '[object Object]');  // true
console.log(0 == -0);               // true
console.log(NaN == NaN);            // false
console.log(Object.is(0, -0));      // false
```

The rule that generates the table: the same types compare directly, `null` and `undefined` are equal only to each other, and anything else converts to a number. The only case worth keeping is `value == null`, which tests for both absence values in one expression.

`Object.is` versus `===`:

```js
console.log(NaN === NaN, Object.is(NaN, NaN));        // false true
console.log(0 === -0, Object.is(0, -0));              // true false
console.log(1 / 0, 1 / -0);                           // Infinity -Infinity
```

Sorting and grouping keys must therefore normalise explicitly:

```js
const rows = [{ v: 1 }, { v: '1' }, { v: true }];
console.log(new Set(rows.map((r) => r.v)).size);        // 3 — the types differ
console.log(new Set(rows.map((r) => String(r.v))).size); // 2 — 'true' is distinct
console.log(new Set(rows.map((r) => Number(r.v))).size); // 1
```

sections.title: Choosing between the equality operators in real code

pages.text:
The strict operator is the default. Use value === null to check for exactly null, and value == null as the single idiomatic loose comparison, because it is true for both null and undefined and false for zero and the empty string. That single exception exists because the two absence values are interchangeable in most code.

Structural comparison has no built-in operator. A shallow field comparison reads: a.id === b.id && a.name === b.name. For arrays, compare length first and then every element, or compare a canonical serialization such as JSON.stringify when the data is JSON-safe and key order is stable. Remember that JSON.stringify ignores key order differences only when the objects were built in the same order, so it is a convenience rather than a specification.

NaN breaks the usual equality rules because NaN === NaN is false. Detect it with Number.isNaN, not with === or with the global isNaN, which coerces its argument and therefore reports true for the string abc. The pattern Number.isNaN(parsed) is the correct guard after a numeric parse.

Sorting comparisons need a number, not a boolean. A comparator returning a.name < b.name yields false in both the less-than and greater-than cases, so the sort silently does nothing. Return a numeric difference, or a -1, 0 and 1 derived from the comparison. For strings in other languages, use Intl.Collator, which knows that accented letters sort near their base forms and that some locales order characters differently.

### Numbers, money and precision recipes

Floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. The demonstration is 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004. For display, format with toFixed or Intl.NumberFormat. For comparison, use a tolerance such as Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON, or better, avoid the situation by not comparing computed floats for exact equality at all.

For money, store the smallest integer unit: cents, satoshi, paise. A price of 19.99 is held as 1999, and all arithmetic stays in integers until display, when a single division by 100 formats the result. Where fractional units are unavoidable, use a decimal library that represents numbers as a coefficient and a scale, because no binary floating point representation can hold 0.1 exactly.

Rounding has several modes and the default surprises people. Math.round rounds halves away from zero for positive numbers, but the negative half case and bankers rounding differ, so a financial calculation must choose deliberately. Math.trunc removes the fraction toward zero, Math.floor goes down, Math.ceil goes up. Formatting with Intl.NumberFormat and a fixed maximum fraction digit count is the safest route to a user-facing string.

Large identifiers exceed the safe integer range and silently lose precision through JSON and arithmetic. Store them as strings end to end, or convert with BigInt for arithmetic and convert back with toString for transport. The failure mode is quiet: an identifier that differs only in its last digits becomes a different, wrong record.

Randomness for anything security-sensitive uses crypto.getRandomValues rather than Math.random. A uniform integer in a range is derived by rejection sampling or by a helper library, because scaling a random float introduces bias near the boundaries and is unsuitable for tokens or lotteries.

chapters.title: Functions, Closures and this — Worked Examples

pages.text:
A counter factory demonstrates captured state: function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }. Each call to counter creates a fresh binding, so two counters from the factory do not share n. This is the mechanism behind private state, memoisation caches and configuration captured at creation time.

A once wrapper shows closure over a flag: function once(fn) { let called = false; let result; return (...args) => { if (!called) { called = true; result = fn(...args); } return result; }; }. The wrapper returns the cached result on later calls, which is useful for expensive initialisation and for idempotent setup.

Memoisation captures a cache keyed by arguments: function memo(fn) { const cache = new Map(); return (key, ...rest) => { if (!cache.has(key)) cache.set(key, fn(key, ...rest)); return cache.get(key); }; }. Two cautions apply. The function must be pure, or the cache returns stale results, and the cache must be bounded for long-running processes, otherwise it grows without limit.

Debounce and throttle are closures over a timer: function debounce(fn, ms) { let t; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); }; }. The captured t is what allows a later call to cancel an earlier one, which is why the timer identifier must live in the closure rather than as a module-level variable shared by every caller.

The classic loop bug is a closure over a var loop variable: with var, every callback shares one binding and all see the final value. Switching to let creates a new binding per iteration, and the callbacks capture the value for their own iteration. This is a specification guarantee, not a compiler trick.

chapters.title: Objects, Prototypes and Classes — Worked Examples

pages.text:
An object literal is right for a fixed shape record: const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ada' }. A factory function is right when construction involves logic or defaults: function createUser(raw) { return { id: raw.id, name: raw.name ?? 'anonymous' }; }. A class is right when many instances share behaviour and identity through a prototype, or when the type is part of the public API.

Object.create is the direct expression of delegation and is useful for prototype-based inheritance without classes: const admin = Object.create(userPrototype); admin.role = 'admin'. Every property lookup on admin that misses falls through to userPrototype, which is how shared behaviour works with no copying.

structuredClone is the correct deep copy for plain data, and it handles nested objects, arrays, Map, Set, Date and typed arrays. It cannot clone functions, class instances lose their prototype, and DOM nodes are rejected. For data with methods, write an explicit clone that reconstructs the instance, rather than hoping a generic copy preserves behaviour.

A plain object is the right dictionary only when keys are known strings and the shape is stable. When keys are dynamic, when frequent additions and deletions occur, or when the key type is not a string, a Map is faster and safer because it does not consult the prototype chain and cannot collide with inherited names such as constructor or toString.
