sections.title: Transforming data with the array methods

pages.text:
A map transforms one-to-one: const names = users.map((u) => u.name). A filter selects: const active = users.filter((u) => u.active). Chaining them reads as a pipeline: users.filter((u) => u.active).map((u) => u.name) returns the names of active users with no intermediate variables and no manual index bookkeeping.

flatMap combines a map and a one-level flatten, which is the tool for turning a list into many items: const tags = posts.flatMap((p) => p.tags). Deduplicating the result is a Set away: [...new Set(tags)]. This pair replaces the manual loop-with-push pattern in most code and produces a stable, readable transformation.

reduce builds a value from a list. Counting occurrences is the canonical example: words.reduce((acc, w) => { acc[w] = (acc[w] ?? 0) + 1; return acc; }, {}). Summing is the simplest: numbers.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0). Always pass the initial value, otherwise an empty array throws, and prefer a Map for grouping when keys are not strings.

The failing callback trap is worth memorising: [1, 2, 3].map(parseInt) returns [1, NaN, NaN], because map passes the index as the second argument and parseInt reads it as a radix. The fix is an arrow wrapper: numbers.map((n) => parseInt(n, 10)). The same trap applies to any function whose second parameter is meaningful.

### Code

Sparse arrays and holes behave differently in every operation, which is why `Array.from` is the safer constructor:

```js
const sparse = new Array(3);
console.log(sparse.length, sparse[0], Object.keys(sparse));   // 3 undefined []
console.log(sparse.map((x) => x ?? 'x'));                     // [ <3 empty items> ]

const filled = Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i);
console.log(filled);                                          // [0, 1, 2]
console.log(Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => 'x'));            // ['x','x','x']
console.log([...Array(3).keys()]);                            // [0, 1, 2]
```

Mutating methods versus their copying counterparts, side by side:

```js
const base = [3, 1, 2];
console.log([...base].sort());          // [1, 2, 3]
console.log(base.toSorted());           // [1, 2, 3]   base unchanged
console.log(base.toReversed());         // [2, 1, 3]
console.log(base.with(0, 9));           // [9, 1, 2]
console.log(base.toSpliced(0, 1));      // [1, 2]
console.log(base);                      // [3, 1, 2]
```

Sort stability and comparator shape decide multi-key ordering:

```js
const rows = [
  { dept: 'a', n: 2 },
  { dept: 'b', n: 1 },
  { dept: 'a', n: 1 },
];
const sorted = rows.toSorted((x, y) => x.dept.localeCompare(y.dept) || x.n - y.n);
console.log(sorted.map((r) => `${r.dept}${r.n}`));   // [ 'a1', 'a2', 'b1' ]
console.log(rows.map((r) => `${r.dept}${r.n}`));     // original order kept
console.log(new Intl.Collator('de').compare('ä', 'z') < 0);   // true
```

Grouping by a key uses reduce or the static Object.groupBy: const byTeam = Object.groupBy(players, (p) => p.team). Before that helper existed, the pattern was rows.reduce((acc, row) => ((acc[row.team] ??= []).push(row), acc), {}). The nullish assignment operator makes the first case concise, and a Map is preferred when the key type is not a string.

Aggregating several results in one pass avoids repeated iteration: const stats = rows.reduce((acc, r) => ({ count: acc.count + 1, total: acc.total + r.amount, max: Math.max(acc.max, r.amount) }), { count: 0, total: 0, max: 0 }). A single pass is clearer here than three separate map and reduce calls, and it is measurably faster for large inputs.

Sorting must be given a comparator for numbers: numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b) sorts ascending, and b - a sorts descending. Sorting strings with the default comparator is code-unit order, which puts uppercase before lowercase and is rarely wanted for display; Intl.Collator.compare gives alphabetical order for a locale. Sorting objects by a field uses the same shape, and sorting by several fields chains comparisons with a fallback.

sort mutates in place, so copy first when the original order matters: const sorted = [...rows].sort(cmp). This one-line difference is the source of many bugs where a table re-sorts its source data and the original order is lost. When sorting is frequent and the data is stable, sorting once on ingest and storing the order avoids repeated work.

### Iterators, generators and sets in practice

A generator expresses a sequence lazily: function* range(start, end, step = 1) { for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i; }. Because it produces values on demand, it can be consumed with for-of or spread and can represent an unbounded sequence that is only as expensive as the consumer asks for.

Generators also implement infinite or paginated sources cleanly: function* paginate(fetchPage) { let page = 1; for (;;) { const items = yield fetchPage(page); if (!items.length) return; page++; } }. A consumer that breaks early stops the requests, which is not possible with a callback-based pagination helper that has already scheduled the next call.

A Set is the right tool for membership and deduplication: const seen = new Set(); for (const id of ids) { if (seen.has(id)) continue; seen.add(id); process(id); }. A Map is the right tool for counting and grouping by arbitrary keys, offering has, get and set with near-constant cost and a reliable size.

WeakMap is the tool for attaching metadata to objects without retaining them: const owner = new WeakMap(); owner.set(element, id). When the element is removed from the document and nothing else references it, the entry disappears automatically. This is the recommended replacement for storing private data as a stray property on a DOM node, which leaks once the node is discarded.

chapters.title: Async and the Event Loop — Worked Examples

sections.title: async and await recipes and error handling

pages.text:
Await inside a loop is sequential and is correct when order or rate matters: for (const id of ids) { await save(id); }. For independent work this is needlessly slow, and the fix is to map to promises and await them together, optionally in chunks to bound concurrency.

Errors from an awaited call are thrown into the surrounding try, so one try around a group of awaits handles the whole sequence. When a failure should not abort the batch, wrap each call individually: const result = await save(id).then(() => 'ok', (err) => ({ error: err.message })). The two-argument then keeps the failure local without a nested try.

A missing await is a silent bug because the promise is created and discarded. Linting rules that require awaiting or explicitly voiding a promise catch it. When deliberately firing and forgetting, attach a catch to avoid an unhandled rejection: void doWork().catch(reportError).

Parallel with a concurrency limit is written once and reused: async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) { const out = []; const queue = [...items.entries()]; const workers = Array.from({ length: limit }, async () => { for (const [i, item] of queue.splice(0)) out[i] = await fn(item); }); await Promise.all(workers); return out; }. This preserves result order while keeping at most limit operations in flight.

### Concurrency, queues and cancellation

An AbortController propagates cancellation into fetch and any custom API that accepts a signal: const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal }); c.abort(). The rejection carries the name AbortError, which must be distinguished from a genuine failure so that a cancelled request is not reported as an error to the user.

Cancelling on unmount or teardown prevents state updates on a discarded component and drops work whose result nobody wants. The pattern is to create the controller in the effect, pass the signal to every request, and abort in the cleanup function, which the framework calls when the component is removed or the dependencies change.

A simple serial queue guarantees that asynchronous steps run one at a time without interleaving: let chain = Promise.resolve(); const enqueue = (task) => (chain = chain.then(task, task));. This is the tool for writing to a shared resource where overlapping writes would corrupt state, and it needs no library.

The event loop ordering that causes confusion is microtask versus task. Promise callbacks and the code after an await run in the microtask queue, which drains completely before the next timer or render. A recursive promise that schedules another promise can therefore starve timers and rendering, so a self-rescheduling loop should end with a task, such as setTimeout with a zero delay, rather than another promise.

chapters.title: Modules and Code Organisation — Worked Examples

pages.text:
A module should hide a decision, not merely group files by type. A module that owns everything about authentication, including its HTTP calls, token storage and error mapping, can change its internals freely because only its small public surface is imported elsewhere. A module that exports twenty unrelated helpers provides no boundary at all.

Named exports are preferred for libraries because they are statically analysable and tree-shakeable, and they let a consumer rename precisely. A default export is convenient for a primary value such as a component or a class, but it makes automated refactoring harder and can hide a large surface behind one name.

A barrel file re-exports from several modules to present one entry point: export * from './users.js'; export * from './teams.js';. Barrels improve the import experience and hurt tree shaking and startup, because importing one name may pull the whole barrel and can create circular imports. Use them at the public edge of a package, not inside every folder.

Cycles arise when two modules import each other. Because bindings are hoisted, one side may observe an incomplete module during evaluation, which usually shows up as undefined at import time. Break the cycle by extracting the shared value into a third module that both import, or by moving the dependency behind a function call that happens later.

Creating a list safely means creating elements and setting text rather than assembling markup: const li = document.createElement('li'); li.textContent = user.name; li.dataset.id = user.id; list.append(li). Using textContent guarantees that a name containing angle brackets is displayed literally rather than parsed as markup, which closes the most common injection hole.

Batch insertion avoids repeated reflow. Appending into a DocumentFragment and inserting the fragment once performs a single layout: const frag = document.createDocumentFragment(); rows.forEach((r) => frag.append(makeRow(r))); table.append(frag). For very large lists, virtualise instead, rendering only the visible window so the document never holds thousands of nodes.

Updating in place is cheaper than rebuilding when the structure is stable. Keep a reference to the node and change its text or class: row.querySelector('.status').textContent = status; row.classList.toggle('error', status === 'error'). Rebuilding the whole list on every change discards focus, scroll position and internal state, which is a visible defect as well as a performance cost.

Reading layout forces the browser to compute it, so interleaving reads and writes causes repeated reflow, known as layout thrashing. Read all measurements first into variables, then perform all writes. When several elements change size, batch the work inside requestAnimationFrame so it happens once per frame.

A fetch helper that checks the status and parses JSON once keeps call sites short: async function getJson(url, options) { const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { accept: 'application/json' }, ...options }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${res.statusText}`); return res.json(); }. Centralising the check prevents the classic bug of treating a 500 response as success because fetch resolved.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter avoids hammering a struggling service: async function withRetry(fn, attempts = 3) { for (let i = 0; ; i++) { try { return await fn(); } catch (err) { if (i >= attempts - 1) throw err; await sleep(Math.min(2000, 2 ** i * 100 + Math.random() * 100)); } } }. Retry only idempotent requests unless the server accepts an idempotency key, and never retry a validation error.

Cancellation should accompany anything the user can abandon. Create an AbortController per operation, pass its signal to fetch, and abort on navigation, on a new search that supersedes the old one, or on a timeout. A superseded request that is not aborted can arrive late and overwrite fresher results, which produces mysterious flicker in search and autocomplete.

Uploading and downloading with progress uses the response body stream: const reader = res.body.getReader(); let received = 0; while (true) { const { done, value } = await reader.read(); if (done) break; received += value.length; onProgress(received, total); }. The total comes from the content-length header when the server supplies it, and progress is meaningless without it.

Always build paths with the path module: const target = join(root, 'data', 'users.json'). String concatenation breaks on Windows and mishandles separators, and join normalises the result. Use resolve when an absolute path is required, and basename and extname to extract the parts rather than splitting on a slash.

Reading a configuration file safely distinguishes absence from failure: try { return JSON.parse(await readFile(configPath, 'utf8')); } catch (err) { if (err.code === 'ENOENT') return defaults; throw err; }. Treating a missing file as an error makes first-run experience painful, while swallowing every error hides a malformed file that should be reported.

A command-line entry point reads its arguments from process.argv, but a real tool parses flags with a small helper so it supports --name value, short aliases and a help text. Validate required arguments and print usage to stderr before exiting with a non-zero code, because a shell script checking the exit status depends on that convention.

Exit codes carry meaning: zero for success and a non-zero value for failure. Using process.exitCode rather than process.exit allows buffered output to flush. Handling SIGINT to clean up temporary files and close connections makes a tool well behaved when a user presses control-C mid-operation.

A minimal emitter shows the pattern in a few lines: function emitter() { const listeners = new Map(); return { on(event, fn) { (listeners.get(event) ?? listeners.set(event, new Set()).get(event)).add(fn); return () => listeners.get(event).delete(fn); }, emit(event, payload) { for (const fn of listeners.get(event) ?? []) fn(payload); } }; }. Returning an unsubscribe function from on is the detail that prevents listener leaks, because the caller can clean up without holding a reference to the map.

Publish and subscribe decouples producers from consumers across a larger system. The difference from a plain observer is that neither side knows the other: a message bus mediates. This makes cross-cutting concerns such as analytics or logging easy to add, at the cost of making control flow harder to follow, so keep the bus narrow and the event names explicit.

A signal or reactive value generalises the observer: a function that returns the current value, records its dependents on read, and notifies them on write. This is the core of every reactive framework, and it explains why reading a value inside a computation is what subscribes to it. Understanding the read-to-subscribe rule removes the mystery from reactivity.

Whatever the mechanism, always provide disposal. A subscriber that outlives its owner keeps the owner alive through the closure and continues to receive events, which causes both a memory leak and duplicate handling. Frameworks expose a cleanup hook that runs on unmount, and hand-written code should return an unsubscribe function and call it.

### Strategy, command and state machines

The strategy pattern replaces a conditional with a lookup: const formatters = { json: (x) => JSON.stringify(x), csv: (x) => toCsv(x), text: (x) => String(x) }; const format = formatters[kind] ?? formatters.text. Adding a format is now adding an entry rather than editing a branch, and the set of strategies can be built dynamically or injected in a test.

The command pattern turns an action into a value: const commands = { rename: (s, p) => ({ ...s, name: p.name }), toggle: (s) => ({ ...s, done: !s.done }) }; const apply = (state, { type, payload }) => commands[type](state, payload). Because actions are data, they can be logged, queued, replayed and reversed, which is how undo stacks and event sourcing work.

A state machine makes illegal transitions impossible: const transitions = { idle: ['loading'], loading: ['loaded', 'failed'], loaded: ['idle'], failed: ['idle'] }; function next(state, event) { if (!transitions[state].includes(event)) throw new Error('invalid transition: ' + state + ' -> ' + event); return event; }. Explicit transitions replace a scattering of boolean flags that can otherwise reach combinations the interface never intended.

A repository interface separates data access from business logic: function makeUserRepo(store) { return { get: (id) => store.read('users', id), save: (u) => store.write('users', u) }; }. The domain calls the interface, a test injects an in-memory implementation, and the production implementation talks to the real database, all without changing the domain.

chapters.title: Common Bugs and How to Fix Them

pages.text:
Comparing a string to a number with the loose operator hides a parse failure: if (count == 5) is true for the string five. Use the strict operator and convert explicitly with Number, then check Number.isNaN. The same applies to sorting, where a comparator that subtracts strings produces NaN and leaves the array in an unspecified order.

Treating a falsy value as absent is the most frequent logic bug in JavaScript. A quantity of zero, an empty string or a false flag all take the else branch, so if (value) is wrong when zero is meaningful. Test explicitly, and use the nullish coalescing operator rather than the logical or when supplying defaults, because an empty string is a legitimate value.

NaN propagates silently through arithmetic, so one bad parse contaminates a whole calculation. Guard at the boundary with Number.isFinite after every parse and external input, and fail fast with a clear message rather than storing NaN and discovering it later in a report.

typeof has two famous inconsistencies: typeof null is object and typeof of a function is function. Use value === null for the null check, Array.isArray for arrays, and a check on the constructor or a brand property for class instances. A generic type check helper centralises these cases and documents the intent.

Debounce and throttle are the first tools for high-frequency events, and caching is the second. A memoised pure function removes repeated work, and a cache keyed by request removes repeated network calls. Measure with a profile before adding either, because a cache that is never hit adds memory cost and complexity with no benefit.

Batch work into one pass. Three separate loops over the same array are usually a single reduce; three sequential awaits are usually one Promise.all; many small DOM writes are usually one fragment. Batching reduces fixed overhead rather than per-item cost, which is why it often produces the largest gains for the least risk.

Do less in the hot path. Move invariant work out of a loop, avoid creating closures inside a tight loop, avoid try-catch in the innermost iteration when possible, and avoid allocations by reusing an object or writing into a preallocated typed array. Keep object shapes stable so the engine can specialise property access instead of falling back to a dictionary lookup.

Perceived performance is separate from measured performance. Render a skeleton immediately, keep interactions responsive by keeping long tasks short, and prefetch what the user is likely to need next. Users judge an application by how quickly it responds to their first action, not by how long a background job takes.

chapters.title: Math, Number and BigInt — Worked Examples

pages.text:
Math is a namespace of static functions, never a constructor; Math() throws a TypeError. It works entirely on IEEE-754 doubles, so every result is subject to binary floating point. Math.round rounds half toward positive infinity, which means Math.round(-0.5) is -0 and Math.round(2.5) is 3 while Math.round(-2.5) is -2 — not the symmetric behaviour most people expect. When you need half-away-from-zero rounding, use Math.sign(n) * Math.round(Math.abs(n)). When you need banker's rounding or decimal precision, do not use Math at all; scale to integers or use Intl.NumberFormat.

The integer helpers are the ones worth memorising. Math.trunc drops the fraction (Math.trunc(-2.7) is -2), Math.floor goes down and Math.ceil goes up regardless of sign. Math.sign returns -1, 0, 1, -0 or NaN, so it is safe to use as a multiplier. Math.abs(-0) is 0 but Math.abs is not a way to normalise negative zero — Object.is(x, -0) is the only reliable test, and 1 / -0 is -Infinity. Math.min() with no arguments returns Infinity and Math.max() returns -Infinity, which is why reduce over an empty array with Math.max as the reducer throws a cannot-convert-Infinity-to-number style surprise in unrelated code.

Math.hypot(a, b) avoids the overflow that Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b) suffers when a or b is near Number.MAX_VALUE, because the intermediate squares would overflow to Infinity. Math.fround rounds to the nearest 32-bit float and is useful when you want to know exactly what a Float32Array will store. Math.clz32 counts leading zero bits of a 32-bit integer and is the fastest way to build a bit-length function. Math.imul does a true 32-bit integer multiply, and it is the standard trick behind fast 32-bit hashing such as Math.imul(h, 31) + c.

Randomness deserves care. Math.random returns a double in [0, 1) with roughly 53 bits of state, is not cryptographically secure, and must never be used for tokens, password resets or anything an attacker benefits from guessing. For integers in a range, Math.floor(Math.random() * n) is slightly biased for large n because the double's range is not an exact multiple of n. Use crypto.getRandomValues with rejection sampling for anything unbiased or security-sensitive. To shuffle an array correctly, iterate from the end and swap with a random index at or below the current one — the Fisher-Yates algorithm — because the common sort with a random comparator is both biased and slow.

Every Math function returns NaN when a required argument is not a number, and NaN propagates through the whole calculation. That makes NaN the natural sentinel for a failed numeric conversion, but it also means a single bad row in a data set silently poisons an aggregate. Validate at the boundary with Number.isFinite and treat NaN as a data error rather than letting it spread. Also note that Math functions coerce their arguments, so Math.max(null, 1) returns 1 while Math.max(undefined, 1) returns NaN — another reason to convert explicitly before you compute.

Performance is easy to get wrong. Small BigInts are fast in modern engines, but every operation allocates a new heap object, so tight loops over millions of small values can be dramatically slower than using Number. Convert to Number at the edges when the values are known to fit in 2^53, do the heavy arithmetic in BigInt only where exactness matters, and convert back. Above roughly a few thousand bits, the cost of multiplication dominates and schoolbook algorithms are replaced by Karatsuba internally, but the constant factor still dwarfs Number arithmetic.

Practical uses are narrower than the hype suggests. BigInt is the correct type for database identifiers that exceed 2^53, for nanosecond timestamps (Date.now() * 1_000_000n), for cryptographic nonces, and for exact factorial or combinatorics output. It is the wrong type for money if the currency has fractional units — scale to integer cents instead and divide only for display, or use a decimal library. It is also the wrong type for a loop counter you only compare against a length, because the mixed-type comparison rules force conversions on every iteration.

chapters.title: Strings, Text and Unicode in Practice

pages.text:
Strings are immutable and every transforming method returns a new string. Methods that search — indexOf, lastIndexOf, includes, startsWith, endsWith — return either a boolean or a position, never a match object. indexOf returns -1 on failure, so a check of if (str.indexOf(x)) is wrong because position 0 is falsy; use includes or compare against -1 explicitly. startsWith and endsWith accept an optional position argument, and endsWith with an explicit length is the reliable way to test a suffix of a slice without allocating one.

The position-based methods are also the allocation-free ones. slice(start, end) accepts negative indices and clamps out-of-range values, returning the empty string instead of throwing. substring swaps its arguments when start is greater than end and treats negatives as zero, which makes it subtly different from slice. substr, the legacy method that takes a length rather than an end index, is deprecated and should not appear in new code. Choosing slice everywhere removes an entire category of off-by-one and sign bugs.

Case conversion is locale-dependent and the default methods are not locale-aware. toUpperCase applies simple case mapping, so the German sharp s 'ß' becomes 'SS' (a length change) and the Turkish dotless i does not behave as a Turkish reader expects. For display and comparison of human text, use toLocaleLowerCase and toLocaleUpperCase with a locale tag. Never use case folding for security decisions: normalising an identifier with toLowerCase is not a substitute for comparing canonical forms, and the Unicode standard does not guarantee that case-insensitive equality is stable across versions.

Padding, repeating and trimming round out the everyday set. padStart and padEnd take a target length and an optional fill string, and they truncate the fill if it would overshoot — so time.padStart(5, '0') on '42' gives '0042'. repeat(n) throws a RangeError for a negative count and can exhaust memory for a huge count, so validate before calling it. trim removes whitespace by the Unicode WhiteSpace and LineTerminator definitions, which includes the non-breaking space and the byte order mark but not every invisible formatting character; zero-width characters survive trim and must be stripped explicitly when normalising user input.

Replacing and splitting deserve their own warning. String.prototype.replace with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence, which contradicts most people's intuition; use replaceAll or a global regular expression for every occurrence. The replacement string interprets dollar sequences — $$ for a literal dollar, $& for the match, $1 for a capture group — so user-supplied replacement text must be escaped or, better, passed as a function. split with an empty string splits into UTF-16 code units rather than characters, which breaks any astral character; use Array.from(str) or the spread operator when you want code points, and split(//u) only when the regular expression has the unicode flag.

Code units versus code points, measured rather than assumed:

```js
const text = 'a😀é';
console.log(text.length);                    // 4 — UTF-16 code units
console.log([...text].length);               // 3 — code points
console.log(text.codePointAt(1));            // 128512
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(128512));   // '😀'
console.log([...text].map((c) => c.length)); // [1, 2, 1]
```

Grapheme clusters are what a human counts, and only `Intl.Segmenter` gets them right:

```js
const segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
const family = '👨‍👩‍👧‍👦';
console.log(family.length, [...family].length);                  // 11 7
console.log([...segmenter.segment(family)].length);              // 1

const words = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'word' });
const tokens = [...words.segment('hello, world!')].filter((s) => s.isWordLike).map((s) => s.segment);
console.log(tokens);                                             // [ 'hello', 'world' ]
```

Normalisation and slugging, in the order that actually works:

```js
const slug = (input) => input
  .normalize('NFD')
  .replace(/\p{M}/gu, '')        // drop combining marks
  .toLowerCase()
  .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
  .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');

console.log(slug('  Héllo,   Wörld! '));    // 'hello-world'
console.log('é' === 'e\u0301');             // false — different encodings
console.log('é'.normalize('NFC') === 'e\u0301'.normalize('NFC'));   // true
console.log([...'😀🎉'].map((c) => c.codePointAt(0).toString(16)));  // [ '1f600', '1f389' ]
```

### Unicode, code points and graphemes

JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, and .length counts code units, not characters. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane needs a surrogate pair, so '😀'.length is 2 and text.length is not a character count. codePointAt(0) correctly returns 128512 for that string while charCodeAt(0) returns the high surrogate 55357. To iterate real code points, use the string iterator: for (const ch of text) or [...text], both of which yield whole code points. Array.from(text) does the same and gives you an array you can index.

Reading positions is the awkward part, because indexOf and slice still work in code units. If you need to map between a code-unit offset and a code-point index, iterate and accumulate. For grapheme-aware work, use Intl.Segmenter with granularity grapheme: the family emoji '👨‍👩‍👧‍👦' is eleven UTF-16 code units, seven code points and exactly one grapheme, because the four person emoji are joined by zero-width joiners. A text field that counts text.length will report eleven characters for a single visible symbol. The same segmenter with granularity word or sentence gives you linguistic tokenisation that respects the locale and is far better than splitting on spaces.

Normalisation is essential before comparing or storing text. Unicode allows the letter e with an acute accent to be encoded as a single code point or as e followed by a combining accent, and the two strings are visually identical but not equal. str.normalize('NFC') composes to the short form and is the right default for storage and comparison; 'NFD' decomposes and NFD is what you want when you strip diacritics, because you can then remove the combining marks with a regular expression using the Mark category. Casefold-plus-normalise is the standard recipe for a case-insensitive equality test that is closer to correct than toLowerCase alone.

Emoji introduce their own rules. A base emoji plus a skin-tone modifier is two code points and one grapheme; a flag is a pair of regional indicators; a keycap is a digit plus a variation selector plus an enclosing keycap. Counting these with .length produces nonsense. Also remember that emoji presentation is font-dependent, so a short string can render at an unexpected width and break fixed-width layouts. When you truncate text for display, truncate on grapheme boundaries using the segmenter and append an ellipsis, never by slicing at an arbitrary code-unit index, which can split a surrogate pair and produce a replacement character.

Escaping is where Unicode meets security. Lone surrogates are valid in a JavaScript string but are not valid UTF-8, so encoding such a string with the standard TextEncoder replaces the surrogate with U+FFFD, which silently corrupts data. JSON.stringify will happily emit a lone surrogate as an escape and the receiving system may then reject the payload. Unicode tag characters and bidirectional overrides can reorder displayed text so that code that looks benign reads differently to a compiler or a reviewer — the classic Trojan Source attack. Strip or reject bidi control characters and unassigned code points from identifiers and from anything that will be displayed as code.

Regular expressions gain three important features from the unicode flag. Without u, '.' matches one code unit and a pattern can match half a surrogate pair. With u, code points are treated atomically and escapes such as \u{1F600} work. The v flag, the successor to u, adds set operations in character classes: [\p{Script=Greek}--\p{Letter}] subtracts, [[a-z]&&[^aeiou]] intersects, and the intersection operator also supports nesting. Property escapes such as \p{Letter}, \p{Number} and \p{Script=Han} require u or v and are the only portable way to ask for a Unicode category rather than listing ranges by hand.

### Text processing recipes

Slug generation has to survive real input. The recipe is: normalise to NFD, strip combining marks, lowercase with the locale, replace every run of characters outside the allowed set with a single hyphen, then trim leading and trailing hyphens. Anchor the pattern with the unicode flag so an astral character counts once. Never use a global replace with a per-character pattern without collapsing, or a title with several consecutive punctuation marks produces a run of hyphens. Store the original text alongside the slug, because slugs are lossy and cannot be reversed.

Title casing is not uppercasing the first letter of every word. Article and preposition rules vary by style guide, hyphenated compounds have their own rules, and all-caps acronyms must be preserved. A practical approach splits on word boundaries with a regular expression that keeps the separators, applies an exception list, and rejoins. Resist the temptation to build a general solution: title case is a house style, so expose the exception list as configuration and keep the algorithm small. The same reasoning applies to sorting names, where family-name-first conventions vary by locale and cannot be inferred from the string alone.

Sanitising user text for display is a rendering concern, not a string concern. Escaping happens at the moment of insertion into HTML, attribute, URL or JavaScript context, and the rules differ for each. Doing it earlier, when storing, is a mistake because the same value may later be used in several contexts. Build small named helpers such as escapeHtml, escapeAttribute, encodeURIComponentForQuery and use them at the boundary. Never attempt to sanitise by removing angle brackets with a regular expression: HTML is not a regular language and the classic bypasses exploit exactly that assumption.

Deduplicating and normalising lists of strings is a common task with a subtle correctness requirement. If you compare with toLowerCase you will merge strings that differ only in case, which may or may not be what you want for identifiers. For display values, normalise with NFC and compare case-folded; for identifiers, compare exactly. Use a Set for the dedupe but keep the first occurrence's spelling, so the output preserves the author's formatting rather than whichever variant happened to sort first. Sorting the result afterwards with Intl.Collator gives a stable, human-ordered list.

Wrapping and truncating for display must account for the fact that monospace assumptions break for CJK text, where a character occupies two columns. Intl.Segmenter with granularity grapheme gives you the units, and a width function that counts East Asian wide and fullwidth characters as two gives the columns. Combining marks, zero-width joiners and variation selectors occupy zero columns. A correct width function is a small table of ranges plus the segmenter, and it is worth writing once because every naive implementation eventually ships a broken terminal table.

Finally, never build SQL, shell commands, or file paths by concatenating strings. Parameterised queries, argument arrays passed to an exec function, and path.join with basename validation are the only safe forms. String manipulation is not a security boundary. Reserve templating for messages and documents you fully control, and treat every value that came from a user, a network response or a filename as hostile until it has been validated against an explicit allow-list of shape and length.

A Date is a single number: milliseconds since the Unix epoch, 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Everything else is projected through a time zone. The value can be at most 8.64e15, roughly plus or minus 100 million days, and anything outside that range is an invalid date whose getTime() is NaN. Critically, an invalid date does not throw; it silently propagates NaN through every getter and through arithmetic, so a parse failure can travel a long way before surfacing as 'Invalid Date' in the UI. Always check Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) immediately after constructing from untrusted input.

The constructor has three entirely different meanings depending on argument shape. new Date(2024, 0, 1) treats the numbers as local components with a zero-based month, so month 0 is January. new Date('2024-01-01') is parsed as UTC because the date-only form has no time zone and the specification says date-only strings are UTC, while new Date('2024-01-01T00:00') is parsed as local time. That asymmetry means the same literal can produce two different instants on two machines. The only unambiguous strings are full ISO 8601 with an explicit offset or Z, and even then engines historically disagreed about non-ISO formats such as '01/02/2024'. Parse explicitly.

Months are zero-based and days of the month are not, so getMonth returns 0 to 11 while getDate returns 1 to 31. Engines normalise overflow rather than throwing: new Date(2024, 12, 1) is January 2025, and new Date(2024, 1, 30) is March 1. That normalisation is genuinely useful — the last day of a month is new Date(year, month + 1, 0) — but it also hides typos. getDay returns the weekday from 0 for Sunday while getUTCDay does the same in UTC. The local getters and the UTC getters are easy to mix, and mixing them is the single most common source of off-by-one-day bugs.

getTimezoneOffset returns the difference in minutes between UTC and local time, with the sign inverted relative to the usual convention: for a time zone ahead of UTC it is negative. The value depends on the instant, because of daylight saving, so it must be queried per date rather than cached. DST transitions create local times that do not exist (the spring forward hour) and local times that occur twice (the autumn overlap). Constructing a date inside a skipped hour yields a shifted instant, and there is no way to represent the ambiguity of the repeated hour at all in a Date. This is the fundamental reason not to store future local wall-clock times as Date values.

Arithmetic on Dates goes through the numeric value. date2 - date1 is a difference in milliseconds, and adding 86_400_000 adds exactly one day of absolute time, which is one hour short or long across a DST boundary. For calendar arithmetic, set components instead: compute the target year, month and day and let the constructor normalise. getTime() and valueOf() are interchangeable and make comparison with < and > work directly. Never use the equality operators on Date objects: two distinct objects holding the same instant are not === because they are different references; compare getTime() values.

Copying and cloning must be explicit. Dates are mutable and passed by reference, so a function that receives a date and calls setHours mutates the caller's object. Clone with new Date(original) or new Date(original.getTime()). The structuredClone algorithm preserves Dates, so structuredClone(date) is a correct deep copy, unlike JSON round-tripping, which turns a Date into an ISO string and loses the type. Date.parse is the static twin of the string constructor and returns NaN for invalid input, while Date.UTC returns a numeric timestamp from UTC components and is the right building block when you want an instant rather than a local component date.

Rounding and comparison are explicit. Temporal.Duration.prototype.round takes a smallestUnit and a roundingMode such as 'halfExpand' or 'trunc', which removes the ambiguity of the hand-written divide-and-floor code that most applications have somewhere. Comparison operators do not work on Temporal objects directly, so use Temporal.PlainDate.compare or ZonedDateTime.compare, which return the usual negative, zero and positive values and therefore drop straight into a sort comparator. That explicitness is the trade-off the API makes for correctness, and it is worth the extra characters.

Array.prototype.sort compares by UTF-16 code unit order, which puts every uppercase letter before every lowercase letter, sorts accented letters into arbitrary positions and places digits and punctuation according to their code points. For human text that is almost always wrong. Intl.Collator encodes a locale's collation rules, and new Intl.Collator('de').compare('ä', 'z') returns a negative value because German sorts the umlaut near the letter a, whereas the code-unit comparison would place it after z. Use the collator's compare function directly as the sort comparator instead of wrapping it, and reuse the collator instance.

The collator options change the answer in ways the locale alone does not capture. sensitivity controls how much difference matters: 'base' ignores case and accents, 'accent' ignores case, 'case' ignores accents, 'variant' (the default) distinguishes everything. numeric: true makes 'item2' sort before 'item10', which is what people expect for filenames and versioned headings. caseFirst: 'upper' puts uppercase first. Ignore-punctuation and usage: 'search' tune the collator for matching rather than ordering. Because these are construction options rather than call options, you need one collator per distinct combination and should build them at module scope or memoise them by key.

String.prototype.localeCompare is the convenience form and takes a locale and the same options object, but constructing a collator per call is significantly slower in a sort over thousands of items. The rule of thumb is: one comparison, use localeCompare; a loop, build a collator. Be careful that localeCompare's return value is only guaranteed to be negative, zero or positive, not specifically -1, 0 or 1, so never test for equality with -1. Equality with zero is safe and is the correct way to ask whether two strings are equal under a given locale's collation.

Locale negotiation is itself a feature. The Intl constructors accept an array of preferred locales and resolve to the best match using the Lookup or Best Fit algorithm, which is what Intl.getCanonicalLocales and Intl.DateTimeFormat.supportedLocalesOf expose. resolvedOptions() tells you which locale was actually chosen, and you should display that rather than the one you requested, so a user who asked for a fallback sees what they got. Passing an invalid locale tag throws a RangeError, so validate user-supplied tags rather than letting a malformed value crash a formatter built at startup.

Sorting stability matters when you sort by several keys. The specification now requires a stable sort, so sorting by the secondary key first and the primary key second produces the expected grouping. Combining a locale-aware comparator for text with a numeric comparator for scores means the comparator must return a number in every branch; a comparator that returns undefined or a boolean silently produces an implementation-defined order. Write the comparator as an explicit chain of comparisons, each one returning the first non-zero result.

Finally, remember that collation is a property of the locale, not of the text. The same two strings can order differently under two locales and there is no universally correct order. For data that must be ordered identically on a server and a client — cache keys, shards, pagination cursors — use code-unit order and document it, because locale-aware ordering depends on the ICU version and can change between releases. Keep the two orderings separate and name them clearly: a display order for humans and a canonical order for machines.
