Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, Intl.ListFormat and Intl.DisplayNames complete the set for user-facing prose. Relative time takes a signed amount and a unit and produces the localised phrase, including the tense; ListFormat joins an array with the locale's conjunction or disjunction, handling the final separator and the empty and single-element cases; DisplayNames turns a language tag, region code, currency or script into a readable name in a chosen locale. Together they remove most hand-written string tables from an application, and they update with the runtime's ICU data instead of going stale in your source.

The common thread is to move every locale-dependent decision into Intl and keep the application logic locale-free. Message text still needs a translation layer, but the grammar around the interpolated values — plural categories, connecting words, name of the language being shown, ordering of a formatted list — should come from Intl whenever it can. That division keeps the translation files small and makes it far less likely that a translator is asked to fix a grammar bug that is really a code bug.

btoa and atob convert between a Latin-1 string and base64. The trap is the word Latin-1: btoa throws an InvalidCharacterError on any code point above 255, so btoa('héllo') throws in some environments and btoa('😀') always does. The correct round trip for arbitrary text is to encode to bytes first and then to base64. In a browser that is btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new TextEncoder().encode(text))), and the reverse is new TextDecoder().decode(Uint8Array.from(atob(b64), c => c.charCodeAt(0))). Node has the shorter Buffer.from(text, 'utf8').toString('base64') and Buffer.from(b64, 'base64').toString('utf8').

The spread form of String.fromCharCode has a second trap: it passes every byte as a separate argument, so a megabyte of data blows the argument limit and throws a RangeError about too many arguments. Chunk the input or, better, use the Buffer or TextEncoder paths that never build an argument list. This is a common intermittent failure that only shows up with large payloads, which makes it easy to ship and hard to reproduce.

Hex is the other encoding you meet constantly. A byte array to a hex string is the map-and-pad idiom: [...bytes].map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join(''), and the reverse is a pair-wise parseInt with radix 16, with validation, because parseInt('zz', 16) returns NaN and a naive loop silently produces a broken array. Hex is case-insensitive on input and conventionally lowercase on output; normalise before comparing digests, since 'AB' and 'ab' are the same value but not the same string.

Binary data in JavaScript is a family of views over one ArrayBuffer. Uint8Array is the general byte array; Int16Array and Float64Array reinterpret the same memory with different widths; DataView gives you explicit endianness control when reading a binary format. Endianness is little-endian on virtually every platform you will run on, but the platform is not guaranteed to be, so a protocol parser must use DataView with an explicit littleEndian flag rather than relying on typed-array views. Also note that TypedArray.prototype.sort sorts numerically while Array.prototype.sort sorts lexicographically, which is a real surprise when you move code between the two.

Base64 has a URL-safe variant that swaps the plus and slash for a hyphen and an underscore and drops the padding. JWT segments, URL parameters and filenames need it, and a standard base64 payload containing a plus will be interpreted as a space if it travels through a query string unescaped. Buffer supports the 'base64url' encoding, and in the browser you translate the two characters yourself. Never assume a base64 string is safe to embed in a URL, an email header or a filename without choosing the right alphabet.

Finally, base64 is not encryption and not compression. It inflates data by about thirty-three percent, so base64-encoding a large binary payload in JSON is a meaningful cost. It is appropriate for small opaque blobs inside a text protocol and for embedding assets in a stylesheet or a document, and inappropriate as an optimisation. If size matters, compress first and then encode, and remember that both steps are reversible transformations with no confidentiality property at all.

Reading a file in the browser and in Node look different but share the pipeline. In the browser a File gives you arrayBuffer(), text(), stream() and slice(); text() decodes as UTF-8, and for any other encoding you must take the arrayBuffer and decode with the right label. In Node fs.promises.readFile accepts an encoding or returns a Buffer, and createReadStream paired with a TextDecoderStream is the streaming form. In both cases the important discipline is to know the encoding at the boundary and convert once, rather than letting untyped strings flow through a pipeline.

Finally, choose the serialisation format deliberately. JSON is UTF-8 by specification and cannot represent binary data without an encoding step. CSV needs an explicit encoding and a delimiter convention, and Excel on some platforms assumes a locale-specific one unless a BOM is present. Newline-delimited JSON is the format to reach for when you want streaming and human readability together: each line is an independent value, so you can process a huge file with constant memory and recover from a corrupt line by skipping it. Whatever you pick, validate by round-tripping a value containing an emoji, a combining accent and a literal newline before you ship.

child_process exposes four entry points with different trade-offs. spawn starts a program and gives you streams for its input and output, which is the choice for large or long-running output because nothing is buffered. exec runs a command through a shell and buffers the whole output into a callback, which is convenient for small commands and dangerous for anything that can produce megabytes. execFile skips the shell and runs one binary with an argument array, which is the safe form. fork is spawn specialised for another Node module and it opens an IPC channel for message passing.

The security rule is absolute: never build a command string from user input. exec, and spawn with shell: true, hand the string to a shell, so an argument containing a semicolon, a backtick or a dollar-parenthesis runs additional commands. Use execFile or spawn with an argument array, where the operating system passes each element as a distinct argument with no interpretation. On Windows the executable name must include the extension and shell built-ins such as dir are not executables at all, which is why cross-platform command execution needs a real path and, occasionally, an explicit shell chosen deliberately rather than by accident.

Exit codes and failure modes need explicit handling. A process that exits with a non-zero code emits 'exit' with the code, and a process that cannot be started at all emits 'error' instead of 'exit', so you must listen for both. When spawn is given an invalid command, the error arrives asynchronously and an unhandled 'error' event crashes the parent. Always attach the error handler before returning the child object, and treat a missing handler on the error event as a defect rather than a nuisance.

Capture output correctly by choosing streams over strings. The child's stdout and stderr are readable streams, so pipe them if you only want to pass them through, attach a data handler if you want to inspect them, and set a maximum accumulated size if you are collecting them. Ignoring stderr hides the most useful diagnostic information in the whole system. Setting stdio: 'inherit' wires the child directly to the parent's file descriptors, which is exactly right for a CLI that runs another tool and wants interactive output to behave.

Timeouts and cancellation are the caller's responsibility. There is no built-in timeout for spawn; use AbortSignal.timeout(ms) as the signal option, which kills the process and produces an AbortError, or set the timeout option on exec and execFile which sends a kill signal. Killing on POSIX sends SIGTERM by default, and a program that ignores SIGTERM will linger, so escalate to SIGKILL after a grace period. If the child spawns grandchildren, the signal reaches only the direct child unless you create a process group, which is a platform-specific detail worth isolating in one helper.

Environment variables are inherited by default and merged with the env option, not replaced. That means a child can see every secret in the parent's environment, so when you run a third-party tool, pass an explicit minimal env. Values must be strings; a number or undefined in the env object either throws or silently disappears depending on the platform, so stringify deliberately. The current working directory defaults to the parent's, and setting cwd is the reliable way to control where a tool resolves its own relative paths.

Working directory and paths are two different things. process.cwd returns the directory the process was started in and can change at runtime; __dirname and the module URL are fixed at load time. Both are absent in an ES module, where you derive them from import.meta.url instead: fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) gives the file path and dirname of that gives the module directory. Resolving a bundled asset relative to the current directory happens to work in development and breaks when a different directory launches the program, which is why asset paths should be derived from the module location or made absolute at startup.

Memory and load hints round out the picture. process.memoryUsage returns heapUsed, heapTotal, external and rss, and rss is the number an operator cares about because it includes the native allocations that a heap profiler does not show. process.resourceUsage gives CPU time and page faults. Tuning the heap with --max-old-space-size is the standard remedy for a container that the default heap limit makes look like it needs far more memory than it really does. None of these calls should appear in a hot request path; read them on a schedule and export them.

Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, so any long synchronous computation blocks the event loop and stalls every other request. worker_threads runs JavaScript on additional threads inside the same process. Each Worker has its own V8 isolate, its own module registry and its own global object, so module-level state is not shared. A worker is started from a file path or an eval string with workerData passed to its constructor, and it signals completion with parentPort.postMessage. The main differences from a child process are cheaper startup and the ability to share memory.

Workers are the right answer for CPU-bound work: image processing, compression, parsing a large file, a cryptographic hash over many megabytes, or a pure algorithm that takes tens of milliseconds or more. They are the wrong answer for waiting on I/O, which should be asynchronous in the main thread anyway. A worker costs a few tens of milliseconds and several megabytes to start, so creating one per request is worse than the blocking it replaces. Create a pool once, keep the workers alive and queue tasks to them.

The thread boundary is a message boundary, so data is structured-cloned on the way across. Cloning is deep, handles circular references and preserves Dates, Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers and BigInt, but it rejects functions, class prototypes and symbols — a plain object arrives as a plain object and loses its prototype. For large payloads the clone itself becomes the bottleneck, which is where transferable objects come in: passing an ArrayBuffer in the transfer list moves ownership rather than copying it, detaching it in the sender. Read the detached buffer and you get an empty one, which is the failure mode to expect when a transfer is accidentally reused.

SharedArrayBuffer allows genuinely shared memory between threads without cloning, combined with Atomics for lock-free coordination. Atomics.wait blocks the worker thread until a value changes and cannot be called on the main thread, which is deliberate — blocking the main thread is never the answer. Atomics.add and friends are the primitives for counters and simple locks. Use this only when the cloned copy is demonstrably the bottleneck; it is a real concurrency model with real data races, and most applications do not need it.

Lifecycle management is where worker code usually breaks. A worker emits 'online' when it starts, 'message' for messages, 'error' for an uncaught exception inside it and 'exit' with the exit code. An uncaught error in a worker does not crash the parent, so without an error handler a worker can die silently and its task hangs forever. Terminating is asynchronous and returns a promise; a worker running a tight loop that never yields will not terminate until it returns to the event loop unless you terminate with a forced option. Always pair a terminate with a timeout guard.

A minimal pool is a queue plus a fixed set of workers, each idle or busy, with the oldest queued task dispatched to the next worker that reports idle. Restart a worker on error rather than trying to reuse it, and cap the queue so memory does not grow without bound under load. A worker that throws on every task and is restarted on every task becomes an expensive crash loop, so count consecutive failures and degrade explicitly — reject the task, or fall back to running it on the main thread — instead of retrying forever.

A stream is a sequence of data delivered over time in four flavours: Readable, Writable, Duplex and Transform. Readable produces chunks, Writable consumes them, Duplex does both independently, and Transform is a Duplex whose output is derived from its input. Every stream carries chunks as strings or Buffers by default, and in object mode as arbitrary values. The whole point is bounded memory: a stream processes a gigabyte with a fixed buffer rather than loading the gigabyte into an array.

Streams have two modes and mixing them is a frequent source of lost data. Flowing mode pushes chunks to data handlers as fast as they arrive. Paused mode holds chunks until you call read. Attaching a 'data' listener switches a stream to flowing, and adding a 'readable' listener switches it back to paused; removing the last data listener does not automatically restore flowing mode. Piping and async iteration both manage this for you, which is why reading a whole file with chunks pushed through a data handler and separately awaiting a chunk in a loop can silently drop the chunks the other consumer took.

Backpressure is the property that makes streaming work. A Readable reports highWaterMark as the buffer size it is willing to have pending; read returns null when nothing is available; a Writable's write returns false when its internal buffer has exceeded its high water mark, and the caller is expected to stop writing until the 'drain' event. Ignoring a false return from write is the single most common stream bug, and it shows up as unbounded memory growth when the producer is faster than the disk or the network. pipe and pipeline honour backpressure automatically, which is most of the reason to use them.

Piping is convenient and error handling is its weakness. a.pipe(b) forwards data and ends b when a ends, but it does not propagate errors from a to b, and it does not destroy b when a errors. That gap is why pipeline exists: pipeline(a, b, c, callback) connects the streams, forwards errors in both directions and destroys every stream on failure, and in the promise form it rejects. Use pipeline, not pipe, for anything with more than one stage, and treat a bare pipe chain as a latent leak. Always give a pipeline an AbortSignal or a timeout when it reads from the network.

Choosing chunk sizes and encodings affects throughput measurably. A larger high water mark reduces the number of system calls and helps throughput on a fast local disk; on a network stream a large mark just increases latency and memory. Reading text streams with setEncoding('utf8') converts Buffers to strings and, importantly, handles characters split across chunk boundaries correctly. The same guarantee is not automatic if you decode each Buffer yourself. For compressed data a larger chunk size is generally better because the compressor has more context, so tune after measuring rather than assuming.

Object mode is a different beast with its own rules. In object mode a high water mark counts objects rather than bytes, and each chunk is an arbitrary value, so the throughput limit is often the per-object overhead rather than the payload. Object-mode streams are excellent for pipelines of transformation over records — parse a line, validate it, enrich it, write it — and terrible for large numbers of tiny values where the stream machinery costs more than the work. For millions of small records, batching into arrays and streaming the batches is usually the fastest correct design.

http.createServer takes a function that receives a request and a response and returns nothing; you write the response through the response object. The request exposes method, url, headers and the body as a readable stream. The response is a writable stream with setHeader, writeHead, write and end. Node's built-in server speaks HTTP/1.1 and supports HTTPS via https.createServer with a key and certificate, and HTTP/2 via the http2 module. For everything else you compose: framing, routing, body parsing, validation and error mapping are your responsibility.

The url on the request is the path and query only, never the full URL, and it is already percent-encoded. Parse it with new URL(req.url, 'http://' + (req.headers.host ?? 'localhost')) to get a URL object, then read pathname and searchParams. Reading req.headers is case-insensitive because the names are lowercased in the Node API, while the raw headers preserve the original casing and order in req.rawHeaders. Duplicate headers are joined with a comma in the standard way except for a short list including set-cookie, which is always an array.

The body is a stream, so reading it means either buffering it or streaming it. Buffering with for await (const chunk of req) gives you an array of chunks to concatenate, and you must bound the total size yourself: a request with no body limit is a trivially exploitable memory exhaustion, because an attacker can send an endless body. Set a maximum, count bytes as they arrive, destroy the request and answer with 413 when the limit is exceeded. Reading the body twice is impossible; if two middlewares both need it, one must buffer it once and give the parsed result to the other.

Response status, headers and body order are fixed: status and headers first, then the body. writeHead can only be called once and must come before the first write. Headers set after the response has started are silently ignored, which turns a late-set CORS or caching header into a subtle bug. For a JSON API, set content-type and content-length before writing, and end with the serialised body. Content-length is required for some HTTP/1.1 clients to avoid chunked framing, and omitting it means Node uses chunked transfer encoding, which is correct but precludes the client computing a progress percentage.

Keep-alive and timeouts control resource usage. The server keeps connections open by default, and the headers keepAliveTimeout and headersTimeout bound how long an idle connection or a slow header block may occupy a socket. The default headers timeout guards against a slowloris attack that opens many connections and sends headers a byte at a time. If you put a proxy in front, its timeouts must be longer than the application's, or the proxy will close connections the application considers healthy and produce sporadic 502s under load. Setting requestTimeout bounds the total time a request may take.

The server should handle the upgrade and clientError events rather than leaving the defaults. clientError fires when a client sends a malformed request; the default behaviour writes a 400 and the event is not fatal, but logging it reveals scanners and broken clients. The upgrade event is where a WebSocket implementation attaches, and if nothing handles it, Node destroys the socket. Both events are the seams where an observability hook belongs, and both are silent by default, which is why they are easy to omit and hard to debug later.

Structured logging means emitting objects, not sentences. A log line of { level, time, msg, requestId, userId, route, durationMs, status } can be filtered and aggregated; a sentence with the same information cannot. Write JSON to standard output, one object per line, and let the platform collect it. Keep levels small and meaningful — debug for development detail, info for state changes, warn for something recoverable, error for something a human should look at — and never log at info level in a loop that runs per item. The one field that pays for itself immediately is a request identifier generated at the edge and propagated to every downstream call.

Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, full credit card numbers or personal data, and do not rely on remembering that. Redaction belongs in the logger itself, applied by key name, so a developer who logs an entire request object by accident still gets the fields stripped. The most common leak is an error object that carries the request body or the headers in a property. Serialising errors requires care anyway: JSON.stringify of an Error yields an empty object because message and stack are not enumerable, so use a serializer that reads name, message, stack and cause explicitly.

Errors should carry context rather than being re-thrown bare. Wrap a low-level error in a domain error that names the operation, and attach the cause so the original stack is preserved; the cause property and the aggregate form are standard now. Answer with a stable machine-readable code and a correlation id, not a stack trace, and log the full detail server-side. An error handler that maps unknown errors to a 500 with a generic message and logs the real one prevents both information disclosure and vague bug reports.

Distinguish operational errors from programmer errors. A missing file, a validation failure and a downstream timeout are operational: handle them, convert them to a response, keep serving. A TypeError from a code path that should be unreachable is a programmer error: log it loudly and let the process crash so the supervisor restarts a clean instance, because continuing in an unknown state risks corrupting data. The visible symptom of getting this backwards is a process that limps along returning wrong answers, which is far worse than one that restarts.

Async context is where naive logging breaks down. A callback scheduled by a timer loses the request context unless you carry it explicitly. AsyncLocalStorage stores a value for the duration of an async operation and restores it across awaits, which is the mechanism that lets a logger attach the request id automatically without threading it through every function. Wrap the request handler in storage.run, store the context, and read it in the logger. The cost is small and the alternative is passing a context object through every layer of the application.

For the client side, capture errors at the top level and attach the build version and the route. A stack trace without the deployed commit is often useless because the source has moved on. Uploading source maps with the release, and resolving them on the server, converts minified frames into real ones. Rate-limit and deduplicate on the client so a render loop throwing every frame does not send thousands of identical events, and close the loop by linking each report to the request id if one exists.

Metrics should be chosen for the questions you will actually ask: request rate, error rate, duration percentiles and saturation of each constrained resource, broken down by the dimensions you use to decide, usually route and status class. Counter, gauge and histogram are the three types, and histograms are what make percentiles possible. Cardinality is the trap: labelling by user id or request id creates unbounded time series that will overwhelm the metrics backend. Stick to a small set of routes and statuses, and use exemplars or traces when you need to find one specific slow request.

The final discipline is to make debugging cheap before you need it. A single request id in every log line, every response and every trace; a version string in the health endpoint; a record of the deployed commit; timestamps in a consistent timezone; and an error tracker that groups by fingerprint. None of these are interesting features and all of them shorten an incident from hours to minutes. Building them is almost entirely mechanical, which is exactly why they get skipped under delivery pressure and exactly why they should be part of the first deploy rather than a follow-up.

Big-O describes how the cost grows as the input grows, discarding constants and lower-order terms. An O(n) algorithm that does a hundred operations per element is slower than an O(n squared) algorithm for every input below a certain size, and that size is frequently small enough to matter. The notation is a tool for comparing growth rates, not a ranking of implementations. The practical question is always: for the sizes I actually see, which approach wins, and where is the crossover point?

The common growth rates in order are constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic, exponential and factorial. Logarithmic algorithms halve the problem each step, so binary search over a million items takes about twenty comparisons. Linearithmic is the cost of a comparison sort. Quadratic appears whenever a loop contains a loop over the same data, and it is the single most common performance defect in application code: an inner lookup that scans an array, a filter inside a map, a nested find over a nested collection. Most quadratic code in real applications is accidental and disappears when a Set or a Map replaces a scan.

Amortised cost is a separate concept from worst-case cost and both matter. Array push is O(1) amortised because occasional resizes are paid for across many cheap operations, but any single push can be O(n) when the backing store grows. A hash map lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case when every key collides. Quoting the average without the worst case is how a system passes load tests and then falls over on adversarial input, so for anything exposed to untrusted keys, treat the worst case as the one to design against.

Space complexity is measured the same way and is often the real constraint. An algorithm that is O(n) in time and O(n) in extra space may be unusable on a device with a small heap, while an in-place version that is O(n log n) in time and O(log n) in space fits. Recursion adds stack space proportional to depth, so a recursive traversal of a deeply nested structure can exhaust the stack where an explicit stack with a heap-allocated array would not. State both dimensions when you choose, and note that strings and objects in JavaScript carry more per-element overhead than a typed array does.

Input size is not always the obvious dimension. For a string algorithm the relevant size may be the number of bytes, the number of code points or the number of grapheme clusters, and the three differ. For a graph the size is usually the number of vertices plus the number of edges, often written as O(V + E), and an algorithm that is linear in V but quadratic in E behaves very differently on a dense graph than on a sparse one. Naming the dimension explicitly is half of getting the analysis right.

Finally, complexity analysis assumes an operation model that the language does not always honour. In JavaScript, array element access is constant time only for a packed array of the same kind of value; a sparse array or a mixed array of objects and numbers can degrade to a dictionary-like store. Property access on an object shaped inconsistently across call sites defeats the engine's inline caches and can cost several times more. The algorithm is the first-order effect and the representation is the second-order one, and both are needed to predict real performance.

Specialised structures earn their place when a specific operation dominates. A heap gives constant-time access to the minimum and logarithmic insertion, which a sorted array cannot match because every insertion is linear. A trie gives prefix queries in time proportional to the prefix length, which a hash map cannot express at all. A doubly linked list gives constant-time removal of a known node, which arrays cannot. Reach for one when the profile shows the operation is hot; before that, the simpler structure with the better constant factor usually wins.

The decisive test is usually not time complexity but the shape of the access pattern. Write down the operations the code performs, how often each one runs, and the size of the collection, then pick the structure whose cheap operations are the frequent ones. This is a five-minute exercise that replaces hours of profiling, and the answer is frequently that the collection is small enough that any structure works and readability should decide. Optimising a hundred-element list with a trie is a cost with no benefit.

A stack is last in, first out, and in JavaScript an array is already a perfectly good stack: push adds to the end, pop removes from the end, and both are constant-time amortised. Nothing else is needed. The reasons to write a Stack class are to make the intent explicit in a domain that is genuinely a stack, and to hide the array so that no caller can reach into the middle. A stack that answers only push, pop, peek and isEmpty documents the intended use and prevents a maintainer from indexing into it.

Stacks appear wherever the most recent unfinished thing is the next thing to do: matching brackets, evaluating a postfix expression, converting infix to postfix with the shunting-yard algorithm, undo histories, depth-first traversal, and the call stack itself. The bracket-matching case is the canonical one: push every opening delimiter, and on a closing delimiter check that the top of the stack is its partner and pop, ending with an empty stack. The version that counts openers instead of pushing characters fails on interleaved types such as a closing bracket that matches an earlier opener.

The most valuable use of a stack in application code is turning recursion into iteration. An explicit stack avoids the call stack limit, which matters for a deeply nested tree or an unbounded directory walk. The transformation is mechanical: replace the recursive call with a push, and the return path with a pop. Order matters — pushing children in reverse gives the same visit order as the recursive version, which is the detail that trips people up when the output silently comes out mirrored.

A monotonic stack keeps its contents in sorted order and answers next-greater or next-smaller element queries in linear time. For each element, pop while the top violates the ordering, then the top is the answer for the current element, then push. This solves the daily-temperatures problem, the largest-rectangle-in-a-histogram problem and span calculations, all of which look quadratic at first glance. Recognising the shape is what matters: a query about the nearest element that satisfies a comparison is usually a monotonic stack.

A stack is also the natural model for a parser. A recursive-descent parser uses the call stack; a table-driven parser uses an explicit stack of states and symbols. In text processing, a stack handles nested structures such as markup tags, code fences and parenthesised expressions, where the requirement is to know the current nesting context and to detect an unbalanced close. Reaching for a counter instead of a stack is only valid when there is a single delimiter type, which is rarely the case in real input.

The failure mode to guard against is unbounded growth. A stack that only ever receives pushes and never pops is a memory leak shaped like a data structure. Any loop that pushes without a matching pop must have a bound, and any parser must decide what to do on an unbalanced close: recover by ignoring, recover by closing the outer context, or reject. Choosing explicitly at design time is much cheaper than discovering the behaviour by feeding the parser a truncated file in production.

Cycle detection is a required safety check. A list that accidentally points backwards turns any traversal into an infinite loop that eventually exhausts memory. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare detects a cycle in linear time with constant space by advancing one pointer by one and another by two and checking whether they meet. The same technique finds the start of a cycle and the length of the repeated segment. In applications, the practical version is usually a visited Set or a depth limit, but knowing the constant-space method matters when the data is large.

Finally, remember that what you actually want is often not a linked list. When the reason for considering one is fast removal from the middle, ask whether an order-statistics tree or a skip list would be more appropriate; when it is ordered iteration with cheap insertion, an array plus periodic sorting may be simpler; when it is a queue, a deque or ring buffer beats a list on memory and locality. A linked list earns its place when the node identity is stable across removals and the order is maintained by relinking, and that is a narrower requirement than it first appears.

A hash table maps a key to a bucket index by computing a hash and reducing it modulo the bucket count. Collisions are inevitable because the space of keys is larger than the space of buckets, so the table must store multiple entries per bucket, usually as a linked chain or as open addressing with probing. The average case is constant time when the keys are spread evenly and the load factor — the ratio of entries to buckets — is kept low. When the load factor exceeds a threshold the table grows and rehashes every key.

JavaScript gives you no direct access to the hash table, but understanding it explains the behaviour of Map, Set and objects. Insertion order is preserved in Map and Set because the specification requires it, which means they are ordered hash tables internally rather than pure ones. Object property order follows a rule: integer-like keys in ascending numeric order first, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols. That rule is why an object with numeric-looking keys does not iterate in the order you inserted them and why a Map is the right choice when order is meaningful.

The load factor is why a hash table lookup can be slower than an array index even though both are constant time. Resizing is amortised but has a visible spike, which is why latency-sensitive code preallocates or warms up. A table sized to a power of two allows the modulo to be a bitwise AND and is what most library implementations use, with the mixing step doing the work of spreading the high bits before masking. A poor mixing function concentrates keys and turns the average case into the worst case.

Hash quality matters most for keys an attacker controls. Strings hash by a deterministic algorithm, so an adversary who can choose the keys can, in principle, force many of them into the same bucket and degrade every lookup to a linear scan. Mitigations are a randomised seed per process and a strong mixing function; modern engines use both, and the string hash in V8 is computed lazily and cached on the string object. When you build a hash table yourself for untrusted keys, include a random per-process seed.

For custom objects, structural sharing and interning reduce cost. A value that is recreated with the same content hashes to the same number if the hash is content-based, but two objects that are not identical have different identity, so a plain object or Map keyed by object reference treats them as distinct. Content-based keying requires you to derive a stable string or number key yourself and to accept the collision risk of the extracted fields. This is a design decision with correctness consequences, not a micro-optimisation.

The practical takeaways are short. Choose a Map over an object when keys are not strings or order matters. Choose a Set over an array for membership. Keep string keys short if you build millions of them, because hashing is proportional to length. Avoid using large composite strings as keys when a small tuple would do, since the hash walks the whole string. And remember that a nested object as a key means reference identity, which is almost never what the author intended.

A two-level Map is sometimes cleaner than an encoded key. A Map from the first component to an inner Map from the second avoids the encoding problem entirely, keeps the components typed, and allows iterating one dimension efficiently. The trade is more allocation and a more awkward delete, which must prune the inner map when it becomes empty. When the components are naturally nested and both are frequently accessed alone, the nested form is the better shape; when the key is read as a whole, the encoded form is.

Hash collisions for derived keys are a correctness question only for fixed-size hashes. If you hash a composite to a 32-bit integer for speed, collisions are possible and must be handled by storing the original key alongside and comparing on retrieval. The two-level pattern of hash then verify is what every hash table does internally, and it is what you must do if you choose a lossy key. A key that is guaranteed lossless needs no verification, which is why the canonical-string approach is the safer default.

Finally, decide the lifetime of any cache keyed by derived values. A Map that grows forever with derived keys is a memory leak that is much harder to spot than one with a single long-lived key, because each entry looks small and reasonable. Add an explicit size bound with an eviction policy, use a WeakMap when the key is an object you already retain elsewhere, and instrument the size. Every unbounded cache is a slow-motion outage, and the only question is how long the growth takes.

A binary search tree keeps the invariant that every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger. Lookup, insert and delete are then proportional to the height of the tree: logarithmic when balanced and linear when it degenerates into a path, which is what a sequence of sorted insertions produces. That degeneration is the entire reason balanced variants such as the red-black tree and the AVL tree exist, and it is why an unbalanced search tree should not be used with ordered input.

Traversal has three depth-first orders with distinct uses. In-order visits the left subtree, the node, then the right, and produces the values in sorted order, which is the single most useful property of the structure. Pre-order visits the node first, which is what you need to serialise a tree so it can be rebuilt. Post-order visits the node last, which is what you need when a computation at a node depends on the results from its children — directory sizes, expression evaluation and dependency resolution all use it.

Breadth-first traversal uses a queue rather than a stack and visits the tree level by level. It is the basis of the shortest path in an unweighted graph, of level-order printing and of any algorithm that wants the nearest node first. The implementation difference from depth-first is a single line: pushing the children onto a queue instead of a stack. Keeping the level boundary explicit, by recording the queue length at the start of each level, is what lets you compute per-level aggregates without extra bookkeeping.

Deletion has three cases and the third is where implementations usually break. A leaf is removed directly. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children is replaced by either its in-order successor — the smallest value in the right subtree — or its in-order predecessor, and then the successor's original position is removed, recursively, which is the one-child or leaf case. Copying the successor's value and deleting the successor is simpler than relinking and is adequate when node identity does not matter, which is most of the time.

Balanced trees are usually unnecessary in application code because a sorted array and binary search cover the read-mostly case and a Map covers the keyed access case. The balanced tree earns its place when you need ordered iteration and logarithmic insertion and deletion together, when you need range queries such as all keys between two bounds, or when you need order statistics such as the k-th smallest. That combination is exactly what a database index provides, which is why the pragmatic answer in a web application is often to let the database do it.

When you do implement one, keep the balancing logic isolated and test the invariant directly. A balanced tree is correct when every node's subtree heights differ by at most a small bound and the search property holds, and both are cheap to check with a recursive validator. Property-based testing with random insertion and deletion sequences finds rotation bugs far more reliably than hand-written cases. The validator itself must be simple enough to trust, because a validator that shares the bug proves nothing.

A compressed trie, or radix tree, collapses chains of single-child nodes into a single edge labelled with a substring. This reduces the node count dramatically for a typical word list and is what a production routing table or a JSON router often uses. The implementation is more delicate because edges must be split when a new key diverges in the middle of an existing label, but the trade is worth it whenever memory matters. A ternary search tree is the alternative that keeps three children per node and stores one character per node, giving a smaller footprint with slightly slower lookups.

A suffix trie indexes every suffix of a text so that any substring query becomes a prefix walk. Building it naively costs quadratic time and memory, which is why the suffix array and the Burrows-Wheeler transform are the practical structures for full-text indexing at scale. This is the layer beneath a search engine: the inverted index maps tokens to document lists, and the FTS index in a database is exactly that, which is why a keyword search using an index is logarithmic and a substring scan is linear.

The practical lesson is to reach for a trie when prefix queries are part of the requirement and for a hash structure otherwise. Most applications need autocomplete once, and a sorted array of strings with a binary search for the prefix range gives prefix queries with far less code and often better cache behaviour. A trie wins when the collection changes frequently, when the strings are long and share prefixes, or when memory for the index is not the constraint. Choose it for those reasons, not because it is interesting.

A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges, and the two standard representations trade memory for lookup speed. An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a collection of its neighbours, which uses memory proportional to the number of edges and is the right choice for sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix stores a boolean or weight per pair, which uses memory proportional to the square of the vertex count and gives constant-time edge lookup. Most real graphs are sparse, so the adjacency list is the default.

In JavaScript the adjacency list is a Map from a vertex identifier to an array or Set of neighbours. A Map keyed by the vertex value handles non-numeric and non-contiguous identifiers without the wasted array slots that indexing by number would create. A Set of neighbours makes duplicate-edge insertion idempotent and edge lookup linear in the degree; an array is smaller and faster to iterate but allows duplicates. For weighted graphs the neighbour value becomes an object or a tuple of target and weight, and iterating it is the inner loop of every algorithm.

Directedness and weights must be explicit in the model rather than implied by the data. One-way edges appear in dependency graphs, in hyperlink graphs and in state machines. Undirected edges are stored twice, once in each direction, and the code that does so must be in a single function so the symmetry cannot be broken. Negative weights change which algorithm is valid, since Dijkstra assumes non-negative weight; a negative edge requires Bellman-Ford, which is slower but tolerant of them and can also detect a negative cycle.

Reading a graph from a table of edges is the usual integration point. Each row names a source and a target and possibly a weight, and the build function should validate that identifiers are present and that no edge references an undeclared vertex. Storing the vertex list explicitly rather than deriving it from the edges matters for isolated vertices, which have no edges and would otherwise vanish. Degree counts, connected components and topological order all need the full vertex set, not just the ones that happen to appear in an edge.

For grid-shaped problems the graph is implicit and does not need to be built. A two-dimensional grid of cells is a graph whose neighbours are the up, down, left and right cells in bounds, and the traversal carries the coordinates rather than a node object. This is the representation to prefer whenever the graph is regular, because storing an adjacency list for a grid wastes memory on a structure that can be computed. The same applies to an ordered sequence of states, where the edges are simply the next index.

Representing a graph also invites the reverse question: do you need one at all? A tree is a graph, but a tree has a unique parent and can be stored as a plain nested object or a flat list with parent pointers, which is far simpler than a general adjacency structure. Reaching for the general tool when the data is a tree, a list or a grid is a common source of unnecessary complexity, and the simplest representation that supports the required operations is the right one.

Binary search finds a value in a sorted array in logarithmic time, and the implementation that is correct is worth memorising: low and high indices, a loop while low is less than or equal to high, a midpoint from the floor of the average, and three branches that either return, set high to mid minus one, or set low to mid plus one. The midpoint must be computed as low plus the floor of the difference divided by two rather than as the average of low and high, because the sum can exceed the safe integer range on huge arrays. Off-by-one bugs in the bounds are the other classic failure.

Binary search also answers questions that are not equality tests. Leftmost and rightmost insertion points, the smallest value satisfying a predicate, and lower and upper bounds over a monotonic function all reduce to the same loop with a different comparison. A binary search over the answer space solves optimisation problems whose feasibility check is monotonic, such as finding the smallest capacity that allows a schedule to complete. Recognising that a predicate is monotonic is what makes that technique available.

Searching an unsorted collection is linear by definition, so the right move is often to build an index rather than search harder. A Set for membership, a Map for keyed lookup, a sorted array plus binary search for repeated range queries, and a database index for anything persisted. Building an index costs one pass and turns every subsequent query from linear to constant or logarithmic. That single decision, made once at load time, is usually a larger win than any improvement to the search itself.

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and combines the results. Every call consumes a stack frame, so the depth is bounded by the runtime's stack size, which in JavaScript is on the order of ten thousand frames and varies by engine and by how much each frame holds. Exceeding it throws a RangeError about the maximum call stack size, and the error is not catchable in a useful way because the stack is already exhausted. Deep recursion over a linked list or a deep tree must therefore be converted to iteration with an explicit stack.

Tail calls are not optimised in JavaScript. A call in tail position does not grow the stack in a language with proper tail calls, but the specification's guarantee was effectively removed before shipping and no mainstream engine implements it. Writing a function in tail-recursive style is still good practice for clarity, but it will not save you from the stack limit. Converting to a loop with an explicit accumulator is the portable form and it is what the engine would do anyway if it supported tail calls.

Divide and conquer is the recursion pattern that pays. Split the input into halves, solve each recursively, combine the results. Mergesort, quicksort, binary search, the closest-pair problem and the fast Fourier transform all follow it, and the recurrence for the running time yields linearithmic or better. When the split is uneven, the analysis changes: a recursion that removes a constant number of elements per step is linear, and one that removes a constant fraction is logarithmic, and confusing the two is how a supposedly fast algorithm turns out to be quadratic.

Memoisation turns an exponential recursion into a polynomial one when the same subproblem recurs. Fibonacci is the standard example: the naive version recomputes each value many times and runs in exponential time, while caching the result per input index makes it linear. The cache must be keyed on everything the result depends on, and the function must be pure for the cache to be valid. A function that reads mutable state or the current time cannot be memoised without including that state in the key, otherwise the cache returns stale answers.

The stack depth itself is often the design constraint. A recursive descent over a deeply nested document needs a depth limit that produces a clear error rather than a crash, and the limit should be low enough to leave room for the rest of the call graph. An incremental parser that maintains an explicit stack on the heap can have a depth limit in the tens of thousands, because heap memory is far larger than the stack, and that is the right design for anything that consumes untrusted input of arbitrary shape.

The most practical advice is to write the recursive version first because it is clearer, then convert to iteration only where the depth is genuinely unbounded or the profile shows the allocations matter. A recursive tree walk over a configuration that is four levels deep is fine forever. A recursive walk over a parse tree built from user input is a stack overflow waiting to happen. The distinction is about the input's bound, not about recursion in general, and it should be a conscious decision rather than a style preference.

An application is easier to change when its dependencies point in one direction. The usual arrangement is a thin edge layer that parses input and produces output, a domain layer that holds the rules, and an infrastructure layer that talks to databases, queues and third-party services. The domain depends on nothing outside itself; the edge and the infrastructure depend on the domain. When that rule holds, the rules can be tested without a network and a database can be replaced without touching the logic.

The practical test of a boundary is the direction of the import. If a module that implements a business rule imports an HTTP framework, a database client or a logger, the boundary is already broken. The fix is to define the interface the rule needs — a function that saves an entity, a function that reads the current time — and let the infrastructure provide it. Passing those in as arguments, or assembling them once at startup, is dependency injection in the plain sense and it needs no framework.

Keep the domain free of transport types. A request object, a result set and a database row are three different shapes and collapsing them into one is what makes an application hard to change. A request arrives, is validated into a domain input, the domain runs, and the result is mapped into a response. Each mapping is a place where a field can be renamed or a type coerced explicitly, and it is also the place where a change in one boundary does not ripple into the others. The mapping functions are boring and they earn their keep over time.

Modules should be organised by feature rather than by technical kind once the project passes a certain size. A directory per technical layer with dozens of unrelated files in each forces the reader to open five directories to understand one behaviour. A directory per feature puts the route, the rules, the queries and the tests for one capability together, which matches how changes arrive. Shared code moves to a common module only when a second feature actually needs it, not in anticipation of a third.

The composition root is the single place where everything is wired. One module reads the configuration, constructs the clients, builds the use cases with their dependencies and returns the assembled application. Keeping it a leaf that nothing else imports means no module can reach around the boundary by importing a configured client directly. It is also the only place that needs to know about environment variables, which makes the configuration contract visible in one file instead of scattered across the codebase.

Finally, resist the urge to abstract early. Two similar functions are clearer than one parameterised function with a flag. A factory, a strategy and an adapter all add indirection, and indirection has a cost that is only repaid when there are genuinely several implementations or genuinely volatile behaviour. The signal to abstract is the third duplication, not the second, and the abstraction should be extracted from working code rather than designed before the code exists. Most of the architecture advice in this chapter is about keeping options open, not about picking a pattern.

State is the source of most bugs in a user interface, and the way to reduce them is to hold less of it. Sort every piece of state into one of four kinds: server data, form input, navigation, and derived values. Server data should be cached with an explicit invalidation policy rather than copied into component state. Form input belongs to the component that owns the control. Navigation belongs to the router. Anything computable from the other three should be computed, never stored, because two copies of the same fact can disagree.

The most common anti-pattern is duplicating server state in local state and trying to keep them in sync with an effect. Fetching data into a component, copying it to another piece of state so it can be edited, and writing it back leads to three versions of the truth and a class of stale-render bugs that are hard to reproduce. Fetch into a cache, derive the display value, and send mutations back through that cache. The mutation response is what updates the cached value, and the update is atomic.

Derived state should be computed during render, not in an effect, and memoised only when the computation is measurably expensive. A filtered list, a total, a formatted label and a validity check are all derivations. Storing them and updating them in an effect is both slower and more error-prone, because the effect introduces a render where the derived value is stale. If the computation is cheap, doing it every render is correct and simpler. Measure before wrapping anything in a memo.

Where you do need a store, keep it small and shaped around the data rather than the components that read it. A store that mirrors the component tree is a sign that the state is in the wrong place. Normalising entities by id with a separate index of ids removes duplication and makes an update to one entity a single write rather than a walk through a nested structure. The selectors that read from the store are the natural place to derive, and they are easy to test in isolation.

For real-time data, decide the reconciliation policy explicitly. A pushed update can be applied blindly, merged field by field with the local version, or dropped for a refetch. Blindly applying a push races with an in-flight mutation and can resurrect a value the user just changed; merging needs a notion of which field is authoritative; refetching is simple and correct but expensive. The honest default for most applications is optimistic local application followed by a reconciliation on the next successful response, with a version or timestamp to discard the older write.

Finally, make the loading and error states first-class rather than an afterthought. A request has at least four states — idle, loading, success and error — and a fifth, refreshing, when there is stale data on screen. Rendering a spinner for all of them discards useful data and flickers; rendering nothing while loading produces a layout shift. Decide how each screen looks in each state, including the empty case, and implement the transition deliberately. The states users complain about are almost always the ones nobody designed.

Validate once, at the edge, and convert to a trusted internal type. After validation, the rest of the code can assume the shape without repeating checks, which removes defensive branching from every function. Two boundaries exist: untrusted input from users, networks and files, and output before it is rendered or sent. Validating between them rather than at every layer keeps the domain clean and the failure messages accurate. A validation that runs in the middle of a computation cannot say which field was wrong.

A schema describes both the shape and the constraints, and it should be declared rather than written as a sequence of if statements. Declarative schemas can be composed, reused across the client and the server, tested independently, and used to generate types. The properties to require are: it produces a typed result rather than a boolean, so the caller does not have to re-read the fields; it collects all failures rather than stopping at the first; it distinguishes missing from present-but-invalid; and it strips unknown fields rather than passing them through, because an unexpected field is how mass assignment attacks begin.

Coercion rules should be explicit and minimal. A query string value is always a string, so a boolean or a number must be parsed deliberately; accepting any truthy string means that the string false parses to true. Trimming should happen before length checks so that whitespace-only input is rejected, and normalisation should happen before uniqueness checks so that two spellings of the same address collide. Where a value is a number, decide whether the empty string means zero or missing, because the two choices have very different consequences in an arithmetic path.

Business rules belong in the domain, not in the schema. A schema can say that a date is a valid ISO string; only the domain can say that it must be in the future, or that an end date must follow a start date, or that a discount may not exceed the order total. Cross-field rules also produce better messages when they live where the fields' meaning is known. The schema guards the type, the domain guards the meaning, and the error message names what the person did wrong.

Error messages are part of the interface and should name the field, the reason and the remedy without leaking internals. Message codes that the client maps to localised text keep the server free of translation and let the interface choose phrasing per context. Returning a map from field path to message lets a form highlight every offending input in one round trip instead of forcing the user to fix one field at a time. A validation that returns 422 with a structured body and a stable code per field is a small amount of work that removes a large amount of friction.

Validate on the client too, but never only on the client. Client validation is a latency optimisation and an accessibility feature; it is not a security control, because the client is entirely under the user's control. Share the schema where the language allows it, accepting that some rules cannot run in a browser — uniqueness, authorisation and anything that needs the database. The duplication that remains should be the server's version being stricter, never looser.

Injection happens when data is interpreted as code in another language. HTML, SQL, shell, regular expressions, JSON, template strings and file paths are all languages a value can escape into. The single robust defence is to keep data out of the code channel entirely: parameterise the query, pass an argument array to the process runner, escape at the point of insertion with a helper specific to the context, and use a real parser rather than string manipulation. Every attempt to sanitise by pattern-matching is a bet against the parser you are trying to outwit.

Cross-site scripting is the highest-frequency consequence and it comes in three variants: reflected, where input echoes back in the response; stored, where it persists in the database; and DOM-based, where client code writes untrusted data into an HTML or URL sink. The defence is contextual escaping at render time — different rules inside an attribute, a URL, a style and a script body — plus a content security policy that blocks inline script and unexpected origins. A CSP is a backstop, not a substitute for escaping, and the two together are what make an injection bug survivable.

Never build HTML by string concatenation. Use a templating layer that escapes by default and requires an explicit marker for the rare case where raw markup is intended, so the editor can see and review every exception. The alternative in a client application is to construct nodes with the DOM API, setting text content rather than innerHTML, which makes the escaping automatic because there is no parsing step. When raw markup is genuinely needed, sanitise it with a maintained library that understands the HTML parser's quirks rather than a homemade tag stripper.

Path traversal is the file-system version of the same problem. A filename from a user must never be joined onto a base directory without checking that the resolved result is still inside that directory. The check is on the resolved absolute path, not on the input string, because .. sequences, absolute paths, symbolic links and platform-specific separators all defeat a string test. Replacing the dangerous sequences is not sufficient; resolve, then compare the prefix, then read the file. Reject anything unusual rather than trying to repair it.

Deserialisation is a code execution surface. Parsing JSON is safe if you then validate the result; evaluating JavaScript, accepting a serialised object graph that reconstructs classes, or trusting a cookie that encodes a session is not. Never call eval, the Function constructor or a template compiler on data. Sign anything the client sends and must not alter, verify the signature before parsing the payload, and treat every field as untrusted even after a successful signature check, because a signature proves origin, not validity.

Rate limiting and size limits are part of the input boundary. A maximum body size, a maximum array length, a maximum string length and a maximum nesting depth each stop a class of resource exhaustion attack. A request that opens ten thousand nested arrays, or claims a hundred-megabyte body, or sends a regular expression that backtracks exponentially, is a denial of service delivered as valid input. Bounding the shape before parsing is far cheaper than bounding the damage after.

TypeScript adds a static type system that is erased at run time. Nothing it checks exists in the shipped output, so a type assertion changes only what the compiler believes and has no effect on the value. That single fact explains the whole discipline: types verify the code you wrote, they do not validate the data you receive. Anything that crosses a trust boundary — a network response, a file, a form field, an environment variable — is untyped at run time no matter what annotation you put on it, and must be validated before it is given a type.

The value of annotations is that they turn an assumption into a checked statement. A function signature documents what it accepts and what it returns, and the compiler enforces it at every call site, including the ones written a year later. That is why annotating the boundaries matters most: exported functions, module interfaces, configuration shapes and API payloads. Annotating every local variable adds noise without adding information, because the compiler already infers it and the inference is usually better than what you would write.

Strictness is where the benefit lives. Enabling strict and its related checks turns null and undefined into first-class cases, forbids the implicit any that silently disables checking, and catches the function parameter variance problems that otherwise appear as a run-time error in a callback. The migration cost is real and concentrated in the initial cleanup, and the alternative is a type system that reports success while the code still throws. Start a new project strict; for an existing one, enable the checks one at a time and fix each wave rather than disabling them when they are inconvenient.

Structural typing means a value is compatible when it has the required members, regardless of where it came from. There is no nominal identity unless you create one. This makes types compose well across library boundaries and it also means a value of the wrong conceptual type can be accepted if it happens to have the same shape — a User and an Admin with identical fields are interchangeable. When conceptual distinction matters, brand the type with a phantom property that only your constructor can create, which makes the compiler distinguish two structurally identical types.

The any type disables checking for everything it touches and spreads through the program because any is assignable to everything and vice versa. Prefer unknown for an untyped value: it accepts anything in but requires a narrowing check before use, which forces the validation to be written. Where a type is genuinely impossible to express, a single carefully isolated any with a comment explaining why is better than many inferred ones scattered through the code. Treat every new any as a decision to be justified, and treat a file full of them as a file whose types are not doing anything.

Finally, keep types and values in step by deriving rather than duplicating. A union of string literals should come from the same constant array the code iterates, so adding a variant cannot be forgotten in one place. A type for a payload should be inferred from the schema that validates it, so the compile-time and run-time notions of the shape cannot disagree. Duplication between a type and a value is the mechanism by which they drift, and deriving one from the other removes the possibility entirely.
